topics.title: The importance of the synagogue
topics.overview: The synagogue is the centre of Jewish community life: a place for prayer, study and gathering. Jews can pray anywhere, but communal worship in a synagogue is especially valued.

bullets: **Bet Tefillah** (house of prayer): where services are held.
**Bet Midrash** (house of study): where the Torah and Talmud are studied, and where children learn Hebrew and Jewish history.
**Bet Knesset** (house of assembly): a community centre for social events, charity and celebrations such as Bar Mitzvah and weddings.
Many Orthodox Jews also call the synagogue a **shul** (from the Yiddish for 'school').
Some prayers can only be said with a **minyan** (ten adults). Orthodox count only men, Reform count men and women.
Jews believe the Shekhinah (divine presence) is with a group praying together.
It holds the Torah scrolls, the holiest objects in Judaism.
It supports Jewish identity, especially for Jews living as a minority in Britain.
The synagogue replaced the Temple in Jerusalem, destroyed by the Romans in 70 CE, as the main place of worship.

notes.h: Not the only place to pray
bullets: Jews believe God is everywhere, so prayer is possible at home, at work or outdoors.
Private prayer is valued, but communal prayer is generally seen as more important because it needs a minyan.
**Worship**: daily services, Shabbat and festival services, and special prayers that need a minyan, such as Kaddish and the Torah reading.
**Rites of passage**: baby naming, Bar and Bat Mitzvah, weddings and prayers for mourners.
**Education**: cheder (religion school) for children, Hebrew classes, adult Torah study (shiur) and a library.
**Community**: youth clubs, groups for older people, kosher meals, charity collections and social action. It is a place where Jews in Britain, a small minority, can meet and support each other.

The synagogue building itself is not believed to be holier than other places in the way the Temple was. It is the Torah scrolls, the worship and the community that make it special. It is called a **mikdash me'at** ('small sanctuary').
There are Orthodox synagogues (many belong to the United Synagogue), strictly Orthodox (Haredi) communities, Masorti, Reform and Liberal synagogues.

In Britain the Reform and Liberal movements merged to form **Progressive Judaism** (members voted in 2025; the union took effect at the start of 2026). Many synagogues still call themselves Reform or Liberal, and AQA uses the word Reform.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: Men are expected to pray with a minyan three times a day, so the synagogue is used every day. It is also a centre of intense Torah and Talmud study.

views.label: Reform
views.text: The synagogue is a community centre for everyone, with men and women taking part equally. Many members attend mainly on Shabbat and festivals and pray more privately at other times.

topics.title: Interior features of the synagogue
topics.overview: The Aron Hakodesh, bimah and Ner Tamid are named by AQA. Each feature has a purpose and a meaning linked to Jewish history and belief.

bullets: **Aron Hakodesh** (the Ark): a cupboard or alcove holding the Torah scrolls. It faces Jerusalem and represents the Ark of the Covenant (Exodus 25:10-22). A curtain (**parochet**) covers it.
**Bimah**: the raised reading platform from which the Torah is read, so everyone can hear. In Orthodox synagogues it is usually in the centre. In Reform it is often at the front.
**Ner Tamid**: the ever-burning light hung above the Ark. It represents God's constant presence and the menorah in the Temple (Leviticus 24:2).
**Torah scrolls (Sefer Torah)**: handwritten on parchment, wrapped in a cover and often decorated with a silver crown or breastplate. A pointer (**yad**) is used to read so the text is not touched.
Menorah (seven-branched candlestick) and the Ten Commandments displayed above the Ark.
Star of David (Magen David) and prayer books (siddurim).
Women's gallery or a separating screen (**mechitzah**) in Orthodox synagogues.
Seats facing Jerusalem so worshippers face the right direction.
The Ark and Torah show the Torah is the centre of Jewish life.
The Ner Tamid reminds Jews that God is always present.
The bimah shows the Torah reading is the high point of the service.
The congregation **stands** when the Aron Hakodesh is opened, out of respect for the Torah. The Ark is opened for special prayers such as Avinu Malkeinu.
Being asked to open the Ark is an honour. The curtain (**parochet**) recalls the curtain in front of the Holy of Holies in the Temple.

The Torah scroll is carried in a **procession** round the synagogue to the bimah. Worshippers touch it with the fringes of their tallit or their siddur and then kiss these, showing love for the Torah (compare Ezekiel 3:3: the scroll 'tasted as sweet as honey').
After the reading the open scroll is lifted high (**hagbah**) so everyone can see the writing.
The reader follows the words with a **yad** (pointer) so that hands do not touch the parchment.
The **Ner Tamid** is never allowed to go out (today it is often electric). It recalls the lamp kept burning in the Tabernacle (Exodus 27:20) and the Temple menorah.
**Bimah**: usually in the centre in Orthodox synagogues, showing the Torah is for everyone and should be heard by all. In Reform synagogues it is usually at the front, in front of the Ark.

**Leader's direction**: in Orthodox synagogues the leader faces the Ark (towards Jerusalem) with the congregation. In Reform synagogues the leader often faces the congregation so they can hear and follow.
**Seating**: Orthodox synagogues have separate seating, with a women's gallery or a **mechitzah** (screen), to avoid distraction. Reform synagogues have mixed seating, with families together.
**Music**: many Reform synagogues have an organ; Orthodox synagogues do not use instruments on Shabbat and festivals.
Neither has statues or pictures of God. Decoration uses patterns, Hebrew words, the Ten Commandments and the Star of David.

topics.title: Worship in Orthodox and Reform synagogues
topics.overview: Orthodox and Reform synagogues differ in language, seating, music, leadership and how often they hold services. Knowing the differences is key for 'different' questions.

bullets: Services are almost entirely in **Hebrew**, with no instruments on Shabbat and festivals.
Men and women sit separately: women in a gallery or behind a screen (**mechitzah**).
Only men can be rabbis, lead services or count in the minyan.
Men cover their heads (**kippah**) and wear a **tallit** (prayer shawl). Married women usually cover their hair.
Services are held every day (three times).
Services use Hebrew and the **local language** (English in Britain).
Men and women sit together. Women can be rabbis, read from the Torah and count in the minyan.
Organs and choirs are allowed, and services are usually shorter.
Wearing a kippah or tallit is a personal choice.
Services are held mainly on Shabbat and festivals.
Both use the Torah reading, the Shema and the Amidah.
Both believe in one God and respect the Tenakh, though they interpret it differently.
A **rabbi** ('my teacher') is a teacher and expert in Jewish law who preaches and guides the community. Any adult Jew who knows the prayers can lead a service.
A **chazan** (cantor) often sings the prayers in Orthodox synagogues; in Reform synagogues the cantor may be a woman.

Other British groups include **Masorti** (traditional, but with some modern changes, such as mixed seating in some communities) and **Liberal** Judaism. In Britain, Reform and Liberal Judaism voted in 2025 to merge as Progressive Judaism (in effect from 2026).

Orthodox Jews believe the Torah and its traditional interpretation come from God, so worship should be kept as it has been for centuries: Hebrew is the holy language, and men and women have different roles.
Reform Jews believe Judaism should adapt to modern life, so they use English so everyone understands, stress equality between men and women, and allow instruments to help worship.
Both see communal worship as important and share the same core prayers.

topics.title: Daily services and prayer
topics.overview: Jews pray three times a day, using fixed prayers such as the Shema and the Amidah. Prayer is a way to praise God, ask for help and keep a relationship with God.

bullets: **Shacharit** (morning), **Minchah** (afternoon) and **Maariv** (evening).
Orthodox men are expected to attend all three, with a minyan.
Reform Jews attend mainly on Shabbat and festivals, though many pray at home daily.
**Shema**: the declaration of faith. Said morning and evening.
**Amidah**: the 'standing prayer'. It has 19 blessings on weekdays: 3 of praise, 13 of requests and 3 of thanks. It is said silently, standing, facing Jerusalem.
**Kaddish**: a prayer praising God, said by mourners; **Aleinu**: closes the service.
Prayers come from the **siddur** (prayer book).
Orthodox men wear a **tallit**, and **tefillin** (small leather boxes containing Torah verses) on weekday mornings.
Prayer must be sincere: **kavanah** means focus and intention.
Prayer is a mitzvah, helps Jews feel close to God and brings comfort and strength.

The Amidah is also called **HaTefillah** ('the Prayer') because it is the central prayer of every service. It is sometimes called the Shemoneh Esrei ('eighteen'), its original number of blessings; a nineteenth was added later.
Worshippers stand with feet together, face Jerusalem, take three small steps forward at the start and three back at the end, and bow at set points, like standing before a king.
It is said quietly, following the example of Hannah, whose lips moved but whose voice was not heard (1 Samuel 1:13). With a minyan, the leader then repeats it aloud.

Weekday structure: 3 blessings of **praise**, 13 **requests** (for example wisdom, forgiveness, healing, a good harvest, justice, the coming of the Messiah, rebuilding Jerusalem) and 3 of **thanks** (ending with a prayer for peace).
On Shabbat and festivals the 13 requests are replaced by one blessing about the holiness of the day, because Shabbat is a day of rest from everyday worries.
Some Reform prayer books add the matriarchs (Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah) to the first blessing and change wording about resurrection and a personal Messiah.
To praise and thank God, to ask for help and forgiveness, and to keep a close relationship with God.

It is a mitzvah: the rabbis link the three daily services to the Patriarchs and to the daily offerings in the Temple (Talmud, Berakhot 26b). Since the Temple was destroyed, prayer replaces sacrifice: 'we will offer the words of our lips' (Hosea 14:2).
Praying together strengthens the community and reminds Jews of what they believe every day.
Prayer may help a Jew feel God's presence, but feeling the Shekhinah is not the only reason for praying.

topics.title: Shabbat in the synagogue
topics.overview: Shabbat services are the main weekly worship in the synagogue and centre on the Torah reading. Orthodox and Reform services differ in style.

bullets: **Kabbalat Shabbat** (welcoming Shabbat) service on Friday evening, with the hymn **Lekha Dodi** welcoming Shabbat like a bride.
The main service is on **Saturday morning** (Shacharit), lasting two to three hours in Orthodox synagogues.
The **Torah** is taken from the Ark, carried round the synagogue and read from the bimah. It is read in a yearly cycle, one portion (**parashah**) each week.
Members are called up for an **aliyah** ('going up') to say blessings over the reading. A passage from the Prophets (**Haftarah**) is also read.
The rabbi gives a **sermon**, and the service ends with Aleinu and often a **Kiddush** (blessing over wine) and social time.
It is a way to keep the Shabbat commandment (Exodus 20:8) and to worship together.
It places the Torah at the centre of the community.
It marks Shabbat as different from the rest of the week.
Orthodox: no instruments or electrical items, mostly Hebrew, men lead the reading and the service is longer.
Reform: organ or choir may be used, English alongside Hebrew, shorter service, women may read from the Torah.
Lekha Dodi welcomes Shabbat 'like a bride', and the congregation turns to face the door for the last verse to greet her.
Before the Torah reading, the Ark is opened and the congregation sings as the scroll is carried round. Seven people are called for an **aliyah** on Shabbat morning.
Because the same portion is read in every synagogue in the world each week, Jews everywhere are studying the same text, which unites them.
A Bar or Bat Mitzvah often happens in the Shabbat morning service, as the young person reads from the Torah for the first time.
A shorter afternoon service (Minchah) includes the start of the next week's Torah portion.
Shabbat worship links to the creation (Genesis 2:2-3) and to the Exodus (Deuteronomy 5:15), the two reasons the Torah gives for Shabbat.

views.label: Reform
views.text: Services may include music, English readings and women reading from the Torah. Some members drive to the synagogue on Shabbat so they can attend worship.

topics.title: Shabbat in the home
topics.overview: Shabbat starts at sunset on Friday and ends after dark on Saturday. It is a day of rest, family and prayer, with rituals at home including candles, Kiddush and Havdalah.

bullets: The home is cleaned and a special meal is prepared before Shabbat. No cooking is done during Shabbat.
About 18 minutes before sunset, a woman (or the family) lights **two candles** and says a blessing.
The family attends the synagogue, then has the Friday meal.
At the meal, **Kiddush** is said over wine, and two plaited loaves (**challah**) are blessed. Children are blessed and songs (**zemirot**) are sung.
No work is allowed. The rabbis listed **39 categories of forbidden work (melachot)**, such as cooking, writing and lighting fires. Many Orthodox Jews also avoid electricity and driving.
It is a day for prayer, rest, family time and study.
Shabbat is a gift from God and a reminder of creation (God rested on the seventh day) and the Exodus.
**Havdalah** ('separation') is said after nightfall on Saturday.
It uses a plaited candle, a cup of wine and a spice box. The spice symbolises the sweetness of Shabbat carried into the week.
The **two candles** recall the two forms of the commandment: 'Remember' (Exodus 20:8) and 'Observe' (Deuteronomy 5:12). The woman lighting them covers her eyes while saying the blessing.
The **two challah loaves** recall the double portion of manna God gave in the wilderness on Fridays, so the Israelites did not have to gather food on Shabbat (Exodus 16).
Before eating bread, hands are washed with a blessing. After the meal, **Birkat Hamazon** (grace after meals) is said.
Parents bless their children, and many husbands sing Proverbs 31 ('A woman of valour') to their wives.
An **eruv** (a boundary, often a wire around an area) allows Orthodox Jews to carry things outside the home on Shabbat; there are eruvim in parts of London and Manchester.
Havdalah ends with wishing each other 'Shavua tov' ('a good week').
It is one of the Ten Commandments and the **sign of the covenant** at Sinai (Exodus 31:16-17).
It remembers **creation** (God rested, Genesis 2:2-3) and **freedom** from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15): slaves cannot rest, so resting shows freedom.
It gives time for family, study and prayer away from work and technology. The writer Ahad Ha'am said: 'More than the Jews have kept Shabbat, Shabbat has kept the Jews.'
Pikuach Nefesh allows Shabbat to be broken to save a life.

views.label: Orthodox

views.label: Reform
views.text: Shabbat is kept more flexibly. Some members drive to synagogue or use electricity, seeing 'work' as whatever stops rest and spiritual renewal.

topics.title: Worship in the home; the written and oral law
topics.overview: Jewish worship also happens at home through prayer, the mezuzah and study. Judaism has the Written Law (Tenakh) and the Oral Law (Talmud), which guide daily life.

bullets: A **mezuzah** (a small case containing the Shema) is fixed to the doorposts of the home (Deuteronomy 6:9) to remind Jews of God's laws.
Jews say blessings (**berakhot**) before and after food, and prayers on waking and before bed, including the Shema.
Home worship includes Shabbat and festival rituals.
Private prayer can be in any language and can be more personal. Women often pray at home as they are not required to attend daily services in Orthodox Judaism.
**Tenakh** is the Jewish Bible, made up of: **Torah** (five books of Moses), **Nevi'im** (Prophets) and **Ketuvim** (Writings, such as Psalms and Proverbs).
The Torah is the most sacred and contains the 613 mitzvot. It is read in the synagogue from a scroll.
The **Talmud** records rabbis' discussions of how to apply the Torah. It contains the **Mishnah** (c. 200 CE) and the **Gemara** (later commentary), and was finished by about 500 CE.
It explains how to keep laws, for example what counts as work on Shabbat, and extends the law to new situations.
Orthodox Jews believe the Oral Law was given to Moses at Sinai alongside the Written Law.
Reform Jews value the Talmud but see it as guidance written by humans, not binding law.

notes.h: More on worship in the home
bullets: On waking, many Jews say **Modeh Ani**, thanking God for returning their soul. Before sleep they say the bedtime Shema.
Blessings (berakhot) are said before eating, after meals (Birkat Hamazon), and on seeing or hearing special things such as lightning or a rainbow.
The home is sometimes called a **mikdash me'at** (small sanctuary): the table is like the altar, and Shabbat and festival meals are acts of worship.
Parents have a duty to teach their children: 'Impress them on your children' (Deuteronomy 6:7). Children learn Judaism mainly through home life.
Private prayer can be in any language and in a person's own words, as Hannah's heartfelt prayer shows (1 Samuel 1:13).
A Torah scroll (**Sefer Torah**) is handwritten in Hebrew on parchment by a trained scribe (**sofer**); one mistake can make it unfit for use.

The Torah often states a law without the details. Example: it commands tefillin ('bind them as a sign on your hand', Deuteronomy 6:8), but the Talmud explains what goes inside them and how to wear them.
The Talmud (Shabbat 73a) lists the **39 melachot**, the types of work forbidden on Shabbat, which the Torah does not list.
The Talmud records **different opinions** and debates, teaching Jews to question and discuss. Later codes of Jewish law (Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, the Shulchan Arukh) are based on it.

Many Jews study a page of Talmud each day (**Daf Yomi**), finishing the whole Talmud in about seven and a half years. Children start learning Torah young: Pirkei Avot 5:21 says scripture at five and Mishnah at ten.
Rabbi Adin Steinsaltz wrote that if the Tenakh is the cornerstone of Judaism, the Talmud is the central pillar.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: Both Written and Oral Law came from God. Talmud study is a religious duty, especially for men, and its rulings guide daily life.

views.label: Reform

topics.title: Ceremonies associated with birth
topics.overview: Jews welcome new babies with ceremonies: Brit Milah for boys and naming ceremonies for girls. They link the child to the covenant and the community.

bullets: Boys are circumcised on the **eighth day** after birth, even on Shabbat, by a trained **mohel** (Genesis 17:12).
It is the sign of the covenant with Abraham. It takes place at home or in the synagogue.
The baby is brought in by the **kvatterin** (godmother) and **kvatter** (godfather) and held by the **sandek** on his knees. A chair is set aside for the prophet Elijah.
The boy is given his Hebrew name. Prayers and a celebration meal follow.
Girls are named at the synagogue, often on the first Shabbat after birth, when the father is called to the Torah.
Many families hold a **Simchat Bat** ('rejoicing for a daughter') or **Zeved Habat** (Sephardi custom) ceremony, with prayers, blessings and a party.
Reform Jews often give girls a ceremony similar to boys' in the synagogue.
The 'redemption of the firstborn son' is held on the 31st day for a first-born son, if he was born naturally (not by caesarean) and neither parent is from a priestly (kohen) or Levite family.
The father gives five silver coins to a kohen to 'buy back' the child (Exodus 13:13; Numbers 18:16).
Brit Milah ideally needs a minyan. A chair is set aside for the prophet **Elijah**, seen as the guardian of the covenant.
The father says a blessing for bringing his son into the covenant of Abraham, and those present reply: 'May he enter into Torah, into marriage (chuppah) and into good deeds.'
If the baby is unwell, the Brit Milah is **delayed** until he is healthy, because Pikuach Nefesh (saving life) comes first.
Some families hold a **Shalom Zachar** ('welcome to the male') gathering at home on the first Friday night after a boy is born.
Some parents whisper the Shema into a newborn baby's ear.

Reform and Liberal Jews also practise Brit Milah, and many hold a **Brit Bat** or Simchat Bat (covenant or celebration for a daughter), which can happen at any time after the birth and may include both parents leading prayers.
A small number of Jews in Britain and elsewhere question circumcision and choose a non-surgical naming ceremony instead, but the great majority of Jewish families keep Brit Milah.
They bring the child into the **covenant** God made with Abraham (Genesis 17).
They give the child a **Hebrew name**, linking them to family and Jewish history.
They welcome the child into the community and express thanks to God for new life ('Children are a heritage from the Lord', Psalm 127:3).

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: Brit Milah is compulsory for boys on day eight. Girls are named in the synagogue on Shabbat or in a simpler ceremony.

views.label: Reform
views.text: Brit Milah is also strongly encouraged. Girls' birth ceremonies are celebrated equally, often in the synagogue and including the whole family.

topics.title: Bar and Bat Mitzvah
topics.overview: Bar and Bat Mitzvah mark when a Jewish child becomes responsible for keeping the mitzvot. The ceremonies differ between Orthodox and Reform communities.

bullets: **Bar Mitzvah** means 'son of the commandment'. It happens at 13, usually on the Shabbat after his birthday.
The boy reads from the Torah (an **aliyah**) and often the **Haftarah**, and may lead parts of the service and give a speech.
He wears a **tallit** and **tefillin** for the first time.
He now counts in a **minyan** and is responsible for keeping the mitzvot himself.
The father thanks God for releasing him from responsibility for his son's sins. A family party follows.
The boy spends months learning Hebrew and Torah reading.
**Bat Mitzvah** means 'daughter of the commandment'. It is typically at 12 (Orthodox) or 12 to 13 (Reform).
In Reform and Liberal synagogues the ceremony is like the boys': reading from the Torah and leading the service.
Many Orthodox communities hold a celebration (sometimes called **Bat Chayil**, 'daughter of worth') with a speech and a meal, but the girl does not read from the Torah in the main service.
A girl's maturity at 12 is based on a belief that girls mature earlier.
It marks the move from child to adult in religious terms.
It links the young person to the covenant and the community.
Jews believe it reflects Pirkei Avot: 'at thirteen, the age for observing the commandments'.
A boy becomes Bar Mitzvah automatically at 13 (and a girl Bat Mitzvah at 12) whether or not there is a ceremony. The ceremony celebrates and marks this change.
The young person may give a **d'var Torah** (a short talk on the week's Torah portion). In some synagogues the congregation throws soft sweets after the reading, wishing them a sweet life.
The father says a blessing ('Barukh shepatarani') thanking God that he is no longer responsible for his child's wrongdoing: the young person now answers for their own actions.
The age of 12 for girls is based on the Mishnah (Niddah 5:6), which treats a girl's vows as valid from twelve years and a day.
Some Reform and Liberal synagogues also hold a **Kabbalat Torah** or confirmation ceremony at about 15 or 16, when teenagers can understand their faith more deeply.
Afterwards the young person counts in the minyan (in Orthodox Judaism, boys only), may be called up to the Torah and must fast on Yom Kippur.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: Bar Mitzvah is a key milestone. Bat Mitzvah is usually celebrated differently, without the girl reading from the Torah in the main service.

views.label: Reform
views.text: Boys and girls have the same ceremony, including reading from the Torah, to show equality. Some communities hold it at 13 for both.

topics.title: Marriage
topics.overview: Marriage is seen as a mitzvah and the foundation of family life. The wedding ceremony is full of symbols and takes place under a chuppah.

bullets: Many couples sign a **ketubah** (marriage contract), setting out the husband's duties to his wife.
In Orthodox tradition the couple may fast on the wedding day and not see each other for a week before, and the groom is called to read the Torah (**aufruf**) on the Shabbat before.
Weddings cannot take place on Shabbat or major festivals.
The wedding takes place under a **chuppah** (canopy), which represents the couple's future home. It is often outdoors or in the synagogue.
The bride may circle the groom (seven times in Orthodox weddings), symbolising building a home together.

The rabbi says blessings over wine. The groom places a plain gold ring on the bride's finger and says the declaration: 'You are consecrated to me by this ring according to the law of Moses and Israel.'
The **Seven Blessings (Sheva Berakhot)** are said, thanking God for creation, joy and love.
The groom breaks a glass with his foot, to remember the destruction of the Temple and that joy is mixed with sadness.
The couple spend a few minutes alone (**yichud**), then there is a celebration with music and dancing.
It is a mitzvah (Genesis 1:28, 'be fruitful and multiply') and the basis for family and Jewish continuity.
The Talmud teaches that a person without a spouse lives without joy.

notes.h: The two stages of the ceremony
bullets: Jewish marriage traditionally has two parts, now joined in one ceremony: **kiddushin** (betrothal, 'making holy'), when the ring is given before two witnesses, and **nisuin** (the marriage itself), under the chuppah with the Seven Blessings.
Before the ceremony the groom covers the bride's face with her veil (**bedeken**), recalling Rebecca covering her face when she met Isaac (Genesis 24:65).
The **ketubah** is signed by witnesses and read aloud under the chuppah. It protects the wife, for example her financial rights if the marriage ends.
After the glass is broken, everyone shouts '**Mazel tov**' (good luck / congratulations).
In Orthodox families the couple celebrate with Sheva Berakhot meals for seven days after the wedding.
'It is not good for the man to be alone' (Genesis 2:18): companionship is part of God's plan.
The Jewish home is where children learn Judaism, so marriage helps the faith continue.
Marriage is called kiddushin ('holiness'): the couple are set apart for each other, and God is part of the relationship.
Orthodox Judaism only conducts marriages where both partners are Jewish; views on mixed-faith marriages vary in Progressive communities.
In Britain the Reform and Liberal movements agreed in 2025 to merge as Progressive Judaism; these communities hold same-sex weddings, which Orthodox Judaism does not.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: Marriage is between a Jewish man and a Jewish woman. Traditions such as the bride circling the groom and separate dancing are kept, and only the groom gives a ring as part of the legal act.

views.label: Progressive (Reform and Liberal)
views.text: Practices are more flexible: both partners may give rings and make declarations, circling is optional or done by both, and same-sex couples can marry in these synagogues in Britain.

topics.title: Mourning the dead
topics.overview: Jewish mourning customs show respect for the dead, support the bereaved and move them through stages of grief. Reform and Orthodox Jews differ on some details.

bullets: Jews believe in burial as soon as possible, usually within 24 hours, except on Shabbat and festivals.
The body is washed and prepared by the **Chevra Kadisha** (burial society) and wrapped in a simple white shroud. A plain wooden coffin is used, showing everyone is equal in death.
Mourners tear their clothes (**keriah**) or wear a torn black ribbon, as a sign of grief.
The funeral is held at the cemetery or a chapel. The **Kaddish**, a prayer praising God, is said by the mourners.

**Shiva** ('seven'): seven days of intense mourning at home. Mourners sit on low stools, cover mirrors, do not work or wear leather shoes, and receive visitors. A memorial candle is lit and prayers are said at home.
**Sheloshim** ('thirty'): the 30 days after the funeral, with fewer restrictions.
**Avelut**: for a parent, mourning continues for twelve months, and the child says Kaddish daily for eleven months.
**Yahrzeit**: the yearly anniversary of the death, when a candle is lit and Kaddish is said.
A gravestone is placed after about a year and an **unveiling** is held.

When they hear of a death, Jews say '**Barukh Dayan HaEmet**' ('Blessed is the true Judge'), accepting God's judgement even in grief (compare Job 1:21, 'The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord').
**Aninut**: the time between death and burial. Close relatives are excused from some mitzvot so they can arrange the funeral.
The body is never left alone: a watcher (**shomer**) stays with it and recites Psalms.
The Torah says a body should be buried 'the same day' (Deuteronomy 21:23), which is why burial is so quick.
At the graveside, mourners and friends shovel earth onto the coffin themselves, as a final act of kindness that cannot be repaid.
Flowers are not usually used. Visitors to a grave leave a small **stone** to show they have been there.
The rituals show respect for the body, which was created by God, and many link burial to belief in resurrection.
The stages let mourners grieve fully at first (shiva) and then return gradually to normal life.

The community supports mourners: visitors bring food, the first meal after the funeral (often including round eggs, a symbol of the cycle of life) is provided by others, and a minyan gathers at the shiva house so Kaddish can be said.
The **Kaddish** does not mention death: it praises God, showing faith even at a time of loss.
Mourners are greeted with: 'May God comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem.'

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: Burial only, never cremation. Strict observance of shiva and sheloshim. Traditionally only men say Kaddish in the synagogue, though some communities now welcome women saying it too.

views.label: Reform
views.text: Burial is preferred, but cremation is accepted by many. Mourning customs are followed more flexibly, shiva may be shorter, and women also say Kaddish.

topics.title: Dietary laws (Kashrut)
topics.overview: Kashrut is the set of Jewish food laws. Jews keep them to obey God and show holiness, but views on how strictly to follow them differ.

bullets: **Kosher** (fit/permitted) food is allowed. **Trefah** (not fit) is forbidden. **Pareve** food (fruit, vegetables, fish, eggs) is neutral.
**Land animals**: only those that chew the cud and have split hooves (cow, sheep, goat). Pigs are not kosher (Leviticus 11).
**Fish**: must have fins and scales. Shellfish are not kosher.
**Birds**: not birds of prey. Chicken, duck and turkey are kosher.
**Blood** may not be eaten (Leviticus 17:11). Meat is salted and soaked to remove blood.
Meat and dairy must not be mixed or eaten together (Exodus 23:19, 'Do not boil a kid in its mother's milk').
Many homes have separate dishes, utensils and sometimes two kitchens. Jews wait a period (often 3 to 6 hours) after meat before eating dairy.
Animals must be killed by a trained **shochet** with a very sharp knife in one quick cut, with a blessing, so it does not suffer (**shechitah**).
Reasons for keeping kosher: obedience to God, self-discipline, holiness, Jewish identity and unity, respect for life.
Meat dishes are called **fleishig**, dairy dishes **milchig**, and neutral foods **pareve**. Fish is pareve, so it can be eaten with dairy, but it is not 'meat'.
Only birds on the permitted list are eaten (for example chicken, turkey, duck); birds of prey are forbidden. Most insects are not kosher.
The rule 'do not boil a kid in its mother's milk' appears three times in the Torah (Exodus 23:19, Exodus 34:26, Deuteronomy 14:21); the rabbis explain this as a full separation of meat and milk.
Packaged food is checked by rabbinic authorities and carries a **hechsher** (kosher certification symbol); in Britain the London Beth Din (KLBD) and other bodies certify foods.
Wine and grape juice must also be kosher. During Pesach extra rules apply (no chametz).

notes.h: Reasons and different views on importance
bullets: The Torah gives the laws as a **chok** (a law to be obeyed even without a stated reason) and links them to holiness: 'Be holy, for I am holy' (Leviticus 11:44).
Keeping kosher brings God into every meal, builds self-control (Maimonides) and gives Jews a distinct identity.
**Orthodox**: kashrut is binding for all Jews; homes have separate sets of dishes and many eat only in kosher restaurants.

**Reform and Liberal**: a personal choice. Some keep a 'kosher-style' home (no pork or shellfish, no mixing meat and milk), some keep none. The Reform Pittsburgh Platform (1885) said diet laws belonged to an earlier age, but many Reform Jews today choose some kashrut to express identity.
Some Jews practise **ethical kashrut**, caring about animal welfare, fair trade and the environment, and some become vegetarian or vegan, which makes keeping kosher simpler.

In UK law, as of 2026, religious slaughter without pre-stunning (shechitah) is permitted as an exemption. Some animal welfare groups argue animals should be stunned first; Jewish organisations argue shechitah is humane. Present both views in an answer about this.

views.label: Reform

topics.title: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
topics.overview: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are the High Holy Days, which begin and end the Ten Days of Awe. They are about judgement, repentance and forgiveness.

bullets: Falls in September or October (1 to 2 Tishrei). It remembers the creation of the world and is the day God judges everyone (**Yom HaDin**).
The **shofar** (ram's horn) is blown in the synagogue as a wake-up call to repent. It is also blown every morning during the month before.
Jews eat **apples dipped in honey** and round **challah** for a sweet year and the cycle of the year.
**Tashlich**: Jews go to flowing water and throw breadcrumbs (or empty pockets) to symbolise casting away sins (Micah 7:19).
Orthodox Jews keep two days. Reform Jews usually keep one.
The ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are a time for **teshuvah** (repentance): asking forgiveness from God and from people you have wronged.
Jews give charity (tzedakah) and try to put right wrongs.
The holiest day of the year (10 Tishrei). Jews believe God seals His judgement for the year.
A **25-hour fast** (no food or water) from before sunset to after nightfall. Also no washing for pleasure, no leather shoes, no perfume, no marital relations and no work.
Many wear **white** (a symbol of purity) and spend much of the day in the synagogue.
Services start with **Kol Nidre**, include confession of sins (**Vidui**) and the **Book of Jonah** (God's forgiveness), and end with **Neilah** (closing) and a long blast of the shofar.
Yom Kippur forgives sins against God. For sins against other people, Jews must first apologise to the person.

The Torah calls Rosh Hashanah a day of 'loud blasts' on the first day of the seventh month (Leviticus 23:24; Numbers 29:1). The rabbis taught it is the anniversary of the creation of the world (or of humanity) and the day of judgement (**Yom HaDin**).

Yom Kippur comes from Leviticus 16 and 23:27: on the tenth day of the seventh month the High Priest entered the Holy of Holies to make atonement for the people, and the people practised 'self-denial'. Today prayer, repentance and charity replace the Temple rituals.

Tradition says three books are opened on Rosh Hashanah: for the righteous, the wicked and the in-between (Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 16b). Jews greet each other with 'May you be written and sealed for a good year' (Shanah tovah).
The shofar is blown with set patterns of notes (tekiah, shevarim, teruah). It is not blown when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat.
Some eat pomegranate seeds (hoping for as many good deeds as there are seeds) or the head of a fish ('to be the head and not the tail').
Torah readings include the birth of Isaac and the binding of Isaac (Genesis 21 and 22).
On Yom Kippur the confession (**Vidui**) is said in the plural ('we have sinned'), showing shared responsibility. The prayer **Avinu Malkeinu** ('Our Father, our King') is said with the Ark open.
Many people who are ill, pregnant women at risk, and children under Bar or Bat Mitzvah age do not fast, because of Pikuach Nefesh.

notes.h: Importance for Jews in Great Britain today
bullets: The High Holy Days are the busiest days in British synagogues; many Jews who rarely attend at other times go to services, and some synagogues need extra venues or tickets.
Schools and employers in Britain often allow Jewish pupils and staff time off; Jewish schools close.
Synagogues run High Holy Day charity appeals, linking repentance with tzedakah.
The festivals give Jews a yearly chance to reflect, put relationships right and start again, which many value even if they are not strictly observant.

views.text: Rosh Hashanah lasts two days, and Yom Kippur is observed with a full fast and many hours of services. Those who are ill are excused by Pikuach Nefesh.

views.label: Reform
views.text: Rosh Hashanah is often kept for one day. Services are shorter and may include English readings, and the emphasis is often on personal reflection and ethics.

sources.use: Use for Rosh Hashanah and the shofar.

sources.text: 'The tenth day of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement... you shall deny yourselves.'
sources.use: Use for Yom Kippur and fasting.

sources.use: Use for Tashlich.

topics.tip: Use the words judgement, repentance, forgiveness and one symbol (shofar, white clothes, fast) with its meaning for each festival.
pitfalls: In 2023 many students mixed up Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. Rosh Hashanah: new year, shofar, apples and honey, tashlich, judgement written. Yom Kippur: fast, white, Kol Nidre, Neilah, judgement sealed.
Yom HaDin means judgement for the coming year, not judgement after death (a 2022 confusion). And Rosh Hashanah is not like secular New Year's Eve.
Tashlich uses breadcrumbs (or emptying pockets) thrown into flowing water, not stones.

topics.title: Pesach (Passover)
topics.overview: Pesach remembers the Israelites' escape from slavery in Egypt. It is celebrated mostly at home with the Seder meal and a week without leavened bread.

bullets: Pesach remembers how God freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt through Moses (Exodus 12). God sent ten plagues, and the last plague killed the firstborn of Egypt but 'passed over' Israelite homes marked with lamb's blood.
It falls in March or April (15 Nisan). It lasts **7 days** in Israel and for Reform Jews, and **8 days** for Orthodox Jews outside Israel.
No **chametz** (leavened food) may be eaten or kept at home. Homes are thoroughly cleaned and the last chametz is searched for the night before.
Jews eat **matzah** (unleavened bread), because the Israelites left in such a hurry that their bread had no time to rise (Exodus 12:39).
Many families use separate dishes for Pesach.
Held on the first night (and second night for many Orthodox Jews) at home. The **Haggadah** is read to retell the story.

The **Seder plate**: **maror** (bitter herbs: bitterness of slavery), **charoset** (sweet paste: mortar used by slaves), **karpas** (vegetable dipped in salt water: tears), **zeroa** (shank bone: the Passover lamb), **beitzah** (roast egg: festival offering and new life).
**Four cups of wine** (freedom), **matzah**, **Elijah's cup** (a cup left for the prophet Elijah, who will announce the Messiah) and the door opened for him.
The youngest child asks the **Four Questions** ('Why is this night different?'), so the story is passed on to the next generation.
It reminds Jews that God saves His people and gives hope for the future.
It teaches children about their history and identity. It is a family and community celebration.
The Israelites were slaves in Egypt. God called Moses at the burning bush and sent him to Pharaoh with the demand 'Let my people go'.

God sent ten plagues. Before the tenth, the death of the firstborn, each Israelite family killed a lamb, marked the doorposts with its blood and ate it in haste with matzah and bitter herbs (Exodus 12). God 'passed over' their houses.

Pharaoh let the people go; they crossed the Sea of Reeds and were free. God commanded that the festival be kept 'for all time' (Exodus 12:14) and that parents tell their children the story (Exodus 13:8).
In Temple times Pesach was a pilgrimage festival when a lamb was sacrificed; today the shank bone (zeroa) recalls this.

**Bedikat chametz**: the night before Pesach, families search the house for chametz by candlelight, often with a feather and spoon; ten pieces are hidden for children to find. Remaining chametz is burned the next morning or sold to a non-Jew.
The **afikoman**: half of the middle matzah is hidden and children search for it; the meal cannot end until it is found and eaten.
The Haggadah describes **four children** (wise, wicked, simple and the one who does not know how to ask), showing the story must be taught to everyone in a way they understand.
Drops of wine are removed from the cup for each plague, so joy is lessened by remembering the suffering of the Egyptians.
The Seder ends with '**Next year in Jerusalem**', expressing hope for the future and the Messianic Age.
Pesach also begins the **counting of the Omer**, 49 days leading to Shavuot, when the Torah was given.

notes.h: Importance for Jews in Great Britain today
bullets: Pesach is one of the most widely kept Jewish festivals in Britain: many Jews who keep few other rituals attend a family Seder.
It strengthens family and identity, as each generation tells the story 'as if they personally came out of Egypt' (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5).
Many families add readings about freedom today, such as refugees and modern slavery, and some synagogues and charities hold communal Seders so no one is alone.
Kosher-for-Pesach food is widely available in British supermarkets in areas with Jewish communities.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: Chametz laws are kept very strictly, with separate Pesach kitchens, two Seders outside Israel and an eight-day festival.

views.label: Reform
views.text: The Seder is central, but the festival is usually seven days and rules on chametz may be followed less strictly. The Seder may include modern readings about freedom today.
