topics.tip: Know the Seder plate items and what each symbolises. For 'different' questions, you could contrast preparation (cleaning the home) with the Seder itself, or Orthodox and Reform practice.
pitfalls: In 2025 many students quoted Exodus but did not name it, losing the source mark. Say 'Exodus 12:14 says...'.
Explain why Pesach is important (freedom, God saving the people, identity, passing on to children), not just describe the Seder plate. Link each symbol to a reason.
Do not confuse Pesach with Easter or say Jews celebrate Jesus at Pesach; Pesach remembers the Exodus from Egypt.

flashcards.q: Name the three Hebrew terms for the roles of the synagogue.
flashcards.a: Bet Tefillah (house of prayer), Bet Midrash (house of study) and Bet Knesset (house of assembly).

flashcards.q: What is a minyan?
flashcards.a: A group of ten adults needed for communal prayer. Orthodox count only men. Reform count men and women.

flashcards.q: Why do some Jews call the synagogue a shul?
flashcards.a: Shul is Yiddish for 'school', stressing the synagogue as a place of study as well as prayer.

flashcards.q: What replaced the Temple as the main place of Jewish worship?
flashcards.a: The synagogue, after the Romans destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem in 70 CE.

flashcards.q: Why might a Jew choose to worship at home rather than in the synagogue?
flashcards.a: God is everywhere, so Jews can pray anywhere. Work, travel or distance may make synagogue prayer difficult.

flashcards.q: What is the Aron Hakodesh?
flashcards.a: The Ark: the cupboard or alcove where the Torah scrolls are kept, facing Jerusalem. It represents the Ark of the Covenant.

flashcards.q: What is the bimah?
flashcards.a: The raised platform from which the Torah is read, so that everyone can see and hear.

flashcards.q: What does the Ner Tamid represent?
flashcards.a: The ever-burning light above the Ark, showing that God is always present (Leviticus 24:2).

flashcards.q: What is a yad?
flashcards.a: A pointer used to follow the text when reading the Torah scroll, so the parchment is not touched.

flashcards.q: What is a mechitzah?
flashcards.a: A screen or barrier used in Orthodox synagogues to separate men and women.

flashcards.q: In which language are Orthodox services held?
flashcards.a: Almost entirely in Hebrew. Reform services use Hebrew and the local language (English in Britain).

flashcards.q: How do Orthodox and Reform seating differ?
flashcards.a: Orthodox: men and women sit separately. Reform: men and women sit together.

flashcards.q: Can women be rabbis?
flashcards.a: Not in Orthodox Judaism. In Reform Judaism, yes, and women can lead services and count in the minyan.

flashcards.q: Are musical instruments used in synagogue worship?
flashcards.a: Not in Orthodox services on Shabbat and festivals. Reform synagogues often use an organ or choir.

flashcards.q: How often are services held in Orthodox and Reform synagogues?
flashcards.a: Orthodox: every day. Reform: mainly on Shabbat and festivals.

flashcards.q: Name the three daily services.
flashcards.a: Shacharit (morning), Minchah (afternoon) and Maariv (evening).

flashcards.q: What is the Amidah and how is it structured?
flashcards.a: The standing prayer. 19 weekday blessings: 3 of praise, 13 of requests, 3 of thanks. Said silently and standing.

flashcards.q: What are tefillin?
flashcards.a: Small leather boxes containing Torah verses, strapped to the arm and head by Jewish men at weekday morning prayer.

flashcards.q: What does kavanah mean?
flashcards.a: Concentration and sincere intention in prayer: prayer should come from the heart.

flashcards.q: When is the Shema said?
flashcards.a: Twice a day, morning and evening. It is the declaration of faith that God is One.

flashcards.q: What is Kabbalat Shabbat?
flashcards.a: The Friday evening service welcoming Shabbat, including the hymn Lekha Dodi.

flashcards.q: What is the high point of the Saturday morning service?
flashcards.a: The reading of the Torah, taken from the Ark and read from the bimah.

flashcards.q: What is an aliyah in the Torah service?
flashcards.a: Being called up to say a blessing over the Torah reading.

flashcards.q: What is a parashah?
flashcards.a: The weekly Torah portion, so the whole Torah is read in a year.

flashcards.q: What is Kiddush?
flashcards.a: A blessing over wine that sanctifies Shabbat, said in the synagogue and at home.

flashcards.q: When does Shabbat begin and end?
flashcards.a: From sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday.

flashcards.q: How many forbidden categories of work (melachot) are there on Shabbat?
flashcards.a: 39, such as cooking, writing and lighting fires.

flashcards.q: What happens at the Friday night meal?
flashcards.a: Candles are lit, Kiddush is said over wine, two challah loaves are blessed, children are blessed and songs are sung.

flashcards.q: What is Havdalah?
flashcards.a: The ceremony that ends Shabbat, using wine, a plaited candle and a spice box.

flashcards.q: Why do Jews keep Shabbat?
flashcards.a: It is a commandment (Exodus 20:8), a day of rest remembering creation, and a sign of the covenant.

flashcards.q: What is a mezuzah?
flashcards.a: A small case with the Shema inside, fixed to the doorposts of a Jewish home (Deuteronomy 6:9).

flashcards.q: What are the three parts of the Tenakh?
flashcards.a: Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).

flashcards.q: What are the Mishnah and the Gemara?
flashcards.a: The Mishnah is the first written collection of the Oral Law. The Gemara is rabbis' later commentary on it. Together they make the Talmud.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between the Written Law and Oral Law?
flashcards.a: The Written Law is the Tenakh (especially the Torah). The Oral Law is the Talmud, explaining how to apply it.

flashcards.q: Why is the Talmud important for Jews?
flashcards.a: It explains how to keep the Torah, applies law to new situations, shows rabbis debating, and guides daily life.

flashcards.q: When is Brit Milah performed and by whom?
flashcards.a: On a baby boy's eighth day by a trained mohel (Genesis 17:12).

flashcards.q: Why do Jews circumcise baby boys?
flashcards.a: It is the sign of the covenant between God and Abraham (Genesis 17:10-11).

flashcards.q: What is a sandek?
flashcards.a: The person who holds the baby during the circumcision.

flashcards.q: How are baby girls welcomed?
flashcards.a: With a naming ceremony such as Simchat Bat or Zeved Habat, often in the synagogue on Shabbat.

flashcards.q: What is Pidyon Haben?
flashcards.a: Redemption of the firstborn son on the 31st day, when the father gives five silver coins to a kohen.

flashcards.q: What does Bar Mitzvah mean and at what age?
flashcards.a: 'Son of the commandment': a boy becomes responsible for keeping the mitzvot at 13.

flashcards.q: What happens at a Bar Mitzvah?
flashcards.a: The boy reads from the Torah and Haftarah, may lead the service, wears tallit and tefillin and gives a speech. A party follows.

flashcards.q: At what age is Bat Mitzvah usually celebrated?
flashcards.a: 12 in Orthodox communities, and 12 or 13 in Reform. Girls are seen as maturing earlier.

flashcards.q: How does an Orthodox Bat Mitzvah often differ from a Reform one?
flashcards.a: Orthodox: usually a celebration or speech without the girl reading the Torah in the main service. Reform: the same as boys'.

flashcards.q: Which source says thirteen is the age for observing the commandments?
flashcards.a: Pirkei Avot 5:21 (Ethics of the Fathers).

flashcards.q: What is a chuppah and what does it symbolise?
flashcards.a: The wedding canopy, symbolising the couple's new home.

flashcards.q: What is a ketubah?
flashcards.a: The marriage contract, setting out the husband's duties to his wife.

flashcards.q: Why does the groom break a glass?
flashcards.a: To remember the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem and that there is sadness even in times of joy.

flashcards.q: What are the Sheva Berakhot?
flashcards.a: The Seven Blessings said at the wedding, thanking God for creation, joy and love.

flashcards.q: What does the wedding ring show?
flashcards.a: An unbroken plain ring symbolises the hope for a lasting marriage. The groom gives it with the declaration 'according to the law of Moses and Israel'.

flashcards.q: Within how long are Jews usually buried?
flashcards.a: As soon as possible, usually within 24 hours, except on Shabbat and festivals.

flashcards.q: What is shiva?
flashcards.a: Seven days of intense mourning at home: low stools, covered mirrors, no work, visits from the community and prayers.

flashcards.q: What is Kaddish?
flashcards.a: A prayer praising God, said by mourners. It does not mention death.

flashcards.q: Put the mourning stages in order.
flashcards.a: Shiva (7 days), sheloshim (30 days), avelut (a year for a parent), then yahrzeit (every year).

flashcards.q: Why do Orthodox Jews not cremate?
flashcards.a: They believe in bodily resurrection and the teaching 'to dust you shall return' (Genesis 3:19).

flashcards.q: What does kosher mean? What does trefah mean?
flashcards.a: Kosher means permitted or fit. Trefah means forbidden or not fit.

flashcards.q: What makes a land animal kosher?
flashcards.a: It must chew the cud and have split hooves (cow, sheep, goat). Pigs are not kosher.

flashcards.q: What makes fish kosher?
flashcards.a: It must have fins and scales. Shellfish and eels are not kosher.

flashcards.q: Why are milk and meat kept separate?
flashcards.a: Exodus 23:19 says do not boil a kid in its mother's milk. Homes use separate dishes and cutlery.

flashcards.q: What is shechitah?
flashcards.a: Kosher slaughter by a trained shochet using a sharp knife in one cut, so the animal feels little pain and the blood drains.

flashcards.q: What is the shofar and when is it blown?
flashcards.a: A ram's horn blown at Rosh Hashanah, and at the end of Yom Kippur, as a call to repent.

flashcards.q: What is Tashlich?
flashcards.a: A Rosh Hashanah custom of throwing breadcrumbs into water to symbolise casting away sins.

flashcards.q: How long is the Yom Kippur fast and what else is forbidden?
flashcards.a: 25 hours. No food or drink, washing for pleasure, leather shoes, perfume, marital relations or work.

flashcards.q: What are the Ten Days of Awe?
flashcards.a: The ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, for repentance and putting right wrongs.

flashcards.q: What does Yom Kippur forgive?
flashcards.a: Sins against God. For sins against other people, Jews must first apologise to the person.

flashcards.q: What does Pesach remember?
flashcards.a: The Exodus: God freeing the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, 'passing over' their homes during the tenth plague.

flashcards.q: What is chametz and why is it removed?
flashcards.a: Leavened food. It is removed because the Israelites left Egypt in such haste that their bread had no time to rise.

flashcards.q: What does maror symbolise?
flashcards.a: Bitter herbs, representing the bitterness of slavery.

flashcards.q: What is the Haggadah?
flashcards.a: The book that tells the Pesach story and guides the Seder meal.

flashcards.q: What is Elijah's cup?
flashcards.a: A cup of wine left for the prophet Elijah, who Jews believe will announce the Messiah. The door is opened for him.

flashcards.q: Give four ways a synagogue is used.
flashcards.a: Worship (services, minyan), education (cheder, Torah study), community and social events, and ceremonies such as Bar Mitzvah and weddings.

flashcards.q: What does 'mikdash me'at' mean?
flashcards.a: 'Small sanctuary': the synagogue as a replacement for the Temple in Jerusalem.

flashcards.q: Which prayers need a minyan?
flashcards.a: Communal prayers such as Kaddish, the public reading of the Torah and the repetition of the Amidah.

flashcards.q: Why is the synagogue important for Jews in Britain?
flashcards.a: Jews are a small minority, so it gives them a place to meet, support each other, educate children and keep Jewish identity.

flashcards.q: What do worshippers do when the Torah is carried round the synagogue?
flashcards.a: Touch it with their tallit fringes or prayer book and kiss them, showing love and respect for the Torah.

flashcards.q: Where is the bimah in Orthodox and Reform synagogues?
flashcards.a: Orthodox: usually in the centre. Reform: usually at the front, in front of the Ark.

flashcards.q: What is the parochet?
flashcards.a: The curtain over the Ark, recalling the curtain before the Holy of Holies in the Temple.

flashcards.q: Why do worshippers stand when the Ark is opened?
flashcards.a: Out of respect for the Torah scrolls, the holiest objects in the synagogue.

flashcards.q: What is a chazan?
flashcards.a: A cantor who sings and leads the prayers in the synagogue.

flashcards.q: Why do Orthodox Jews keep services in Hebrew?
flashcards.a: Hebrew is the holy language of the Torah and prayer, and it unites Jews worldwide.

flashcards.q: Why do Reform synagogues use English as well as Hebrew?
flashcards.a: So that everyone can understand and pray with kavanah (concentration).

flashcards.q: What happened to Reform and Liberal Judaism in Britain in 2025?
flashcards.a: They merged to form Progressive Judaism. Many synagogues still call themselves Reform or Liberal.

flashcards.q: Why is the Amidah said standing with feet together?
flashcards.a: As if standing before God the King; feet together copies the angels in Ezekiel's vision. Worshippers face Jerusalem.

flashcards.q: Why is the Amidah said quietly?
flashcards.a: Following Hannah, who prayed silently with only her lips moving (1 Samuel 1:13); it shows prayer is personal and sincere.

flashcards.q: How does the Shabbat Amidah differ from the weekday one?
flashcards.a: The 13 requests are replaced by one blessing about the holiness of Shabbat, so worshippers rest from everyday worries.

flashcards.q: Which verse shows prayer replacing Temple sacrifice?
flashcards.a: Hosea 14:2: 'we will offer the words of our lips' instead of bulls.

flashcards.q: Give three reasons why Jews pray.
flashcards.a: To praise and thank God, to ask for help or forgiveness, and because it is a mitzvah that builds the relationship with God and the community.

flashcards.q: How many people are called up for an aliyah on Shabbat morning?
flashcards.a: Seven (plus one for the Haftarah reading).

flashcards.q: Why do Orthodox Jews walk to the synagogue on Shabbat?
flashcards.a: Driving involves lighting a fire (the engine), one of the 39 forbidden kinds of work.

flashcards.q: Why does reading the same Torah portion each week matter?
flashcards.a: Jews all over the world study the same passage, which unites the Jewish people.

flashcards.q: What two events does Shabbat remember, according to the Torah?
flashcards.a: Creation, when God rested (Exodus 20:11), and freedom from slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15).

flashcards.q: What do the two Shabbat candles represent?
flashcards.a: The two commands about Shabbat: 'Remember' (Exodus 20:8) and 'Observe' (Deuteronomy 5:12).

flashcards.q: Why are there two challah loaves?
flashcards.a: To remember the double portion of manna God provided on Fridays in the wilderness (Exodus 16).

flashcards.q: What is an eruv?
flashcards.a: A boundary around an area that allows Orthodox Jews to carry things outside on Shabbat; there are eruvim in parts of London and Manchester.

flashcards.q: Why does Deuteronomy link Shabbat to Egypt?
flashcards.a: Because the Israelites were slaves and God freed them; resting on Shabbat celebrates freedom (Deuteronomy 5:15).

flashcards.q: What is Modeh Ani?
flashcards.a: A short prayer said on waking, thanking God for returning one's soul.

flashcards.q: What is a sofer?
flashcards.a: A trained scribe who handwrites Torah scrolls, mezuzot and tefillin on parchment.

flashcards.q: Give an example of the Talmud explaining a Torah law.
flashcards.a: The Torah forbids work on Shabbat; the Talmud lists the 39 melachot. The Torah commands tefillin; the Talmud explains how to make and wear them.

flashcards.q: What is Daf Yomi?
flashcards.a: Studying one page of Talmud a day, completing it in about seven and a half years.

flashcards.q: What did Rabbi Adin Steinsaltz say about the Talmud?
flashcards.a: If the Tenakh is the cornerstone of Judaism, the Talmud is the central pillar.

flashcards.q: What do people say to the baby's family at a Brit Milah?
flashcards.a: 'May he enter into Torah, into marriage (chuppah) and into good deeds.'

flashcards.q: Why might a Brit Milah be delayed?
flashcards.a: If the baby is unwell: Pikuach Nefesh (health and life) comes first.

flashcards.q: What is a Shalom Zachar?
flashcards.a: A gathering on the first Friday night after a boy is born to welcome him into the community.

flashcards.q: What is a Brit Bat?
flashcards.a: A 'covenant of a daughter' ceremony welcoming a baby girl, common in Reform and Liberal Judaism.

flashcards.q: Does a boy need a ceremony to become Bar Mitzvah?
flashcards.a: No. He becomes Bar Mitzvah automatically at 13; the ceremony celebrates this.

flashcards.q: What is a d'var Torah?
flashcards.a: A short talk on the week's Torah portion, often given by the Bar or Bat Mitzvah.

flashcards.q: Why are sweets sometimes thrown at a Bar or Bat Mitzvah?
flashcards.a: To wish the young person a sweet life after they read from the Torah.

flashcards.q: What does the father's blessing at a Bar Mitzvah mean?
flashcards.a: He thanks God he is no longer responsible for his son's wrongdoing; the son is now responsible himself.

flashcards.q: What are kiddushin and nisuin?
flashcards.a: The two stages of a Jewish marriage: kiddushin (betrothal with the ring before witnesses) and nisuin (the marriage under the chuppah with the Seven Blessings).

flashcards.q: What is the bedeken and why is it done?
flashcards.a: The groom veils the bride before the ceremony, recalling Rebecca covering her face when she met Isaac (Genesis 24:65).

flashcards.q: Why is the ketubah important?
flashcards.a: It is the marriage contract, signed by witnesses, that protects the wife's rights, including financially if the marriage ends.

flashcards.q: What does 'kiddushin' mean and why is it used for marriage?
flashcards.a: 'Holiness' or 'making holy': the couple are set apart for each other, making marriage a holy relationship.

flashcards.q: What do Jews say when they hear of a death?
flashcards.a: 'Barukh Dayan HaEmet': 'Blessed is the true Judge'.

flashcards.q: Why do mourners and friends shovel earth onto the coffin?
flashcards.a: It is a final act of kindness (chesed) for someone who can never repay it.

flashcards.q: Why do Jewish visitors leave a stone on a grave?
flashcards.a: To show they have visited and remembered the person; stones last, unlike flowers.

flashcards.q: What does the Kaddish prayer actually say?
flashcards.a: It praises God's greatness and asks for peace; it does not mention death, showing faith in God even in grief.

flashcards.q: What is aninut?
flashcards.a: The time between death and burial, when close relatives are excused some mitzvot to arrange the funeral.

flashcards.q: What do fleishig, milchig and pareve mean?
flashcards.a: Meat foods, dairy foods and neutral foods (such as fruit, vegetables, eggs and fish).

flashcards.q: What is a hechsher?
flashcards.a: A kosher certification symbol on packaged food, for example from the London Beth Din (KLBD).

flashcards.q: What does Leviticus 11:44 give as the reason for food laws?
flashcards.a: 'Be holy, for I am holy': keeping kashrut sets Jews apart for God.

flashcards.q: What is 'ethical kashrut'?
flashcards.a: Applying Jewish values to food choices, such as animal welfare, fair trade and the environment, sometimes leading to vegetarianism.

flashcards.q: How do many Reform Jews approach kashrut?
flashcards.a: As a personal choice: some keep a kosher-style home (no pork, shellfish or mixing meat and milk), others keep none.

flashcards.q: What happened on Yom Kippur in the Temple?
flashcards.a: The High Priest entered the Holy of Holies to make atonement for the people (Leviticus 16).

flashcards.q: Why do Jews eat pomegranate seeds at Rosh Hashanah?
flashcards.a: To hope their good deeds in the year ahead will be as many as the seeds.

flashcards.q: Why is the Yom Kippur confession said as 'we have sinned'?
flashcards.a: It is in the plural, showing the community shares responsibility and prays together.

flashcards.q: Who does not have to fast on Yom Kippur?
flashcards.a: People who are ill, those whose health would be at risk, and children: Pikuach Nefesh comes first.

flashcards.q: Why are the High Holy Days important for Jews in Britain today?
flashcards.a: Synagogues are fullest then; they are a time for reflection, putting things right, charity appeals and starting again.

flashcards.q: What is bedikat chametz?
flashcards.a: The search for chametz by candlelight on the night before Pesach; leftover chametz is burned or sold.

flashcards.q: What is the afikoman?
flashcards.a: Half of the middle matzah, hidden during the Seder; children search for it and the meal ends with eating it.

flashcards.q: Why are drops of wine removed for each plague?
flashcards.a: To lessen joy by remembering the suffering of the Egyptians: no one should rejoice fully at others' suffering.

flashcards.q: Which verse commands parents to tell their children the Pesach story?
flashcards.a: Exodus 13:8: 'You shall explain to your child on that day...'

flashcards.q: What does 'Next year in Jerusalem' express?
flashcards.a: Hope for the future, the return to Jerusalem and the coming of the Messianic Age.

quiz.q: Which one of the following means 'house of study'?
quiz.why: Bet Midrash means house of study. Bet Tefillah is house of prayer and Bet Knesset is house of assembly.

quiz.q: How many adults are needed for a minyan?
quiz.why: A minyan is ten adults. Orthodox count only men, Reform count men and women.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is the ever-burning light in a synagogue?
quiz.why: The Ner Tamid hangs above the Ark and shows God is always present.

quiz.q: Where are the Torah scrolls kept in a synagogue?
quiz.why: The Torah scrolls are kept in the Aron Hakodesh (the Ark).

quiz.q: A Jewish worshipper reads from the Torah at the raised platform. What is it called?
quiz.why: The bimah is the reading platform from which the Torah is read.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is true of Reform synagogues?
options: Men and women can sit together
quiz.why: In Reform synagogues men and women sit together, and women can be rabbis.

quiz.q: Which one of these is a feature of Orthodox worship?
options: An organ is used on Shabbat
quiz.why: Orthodox Jews hold services every day, while Reform services are mainly on Shabbat and festivals.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is the 'standing prayer'?
quiz.why: The Amidah is said standing, facing Jerusalem.

quiz.q: What are tefillin?
quiz.why: Tefillin are small leather boxes with Torah verses worn on the arm and head in weekday morning prayer.

quiz.q: What does kavanah mean?
quiz.why: Kavanah is sincere focus in prayer. Maimonides said prayer without devotion is not prayer.

quiz.q: On which day is the main Shabbat service held in the synagogue?
quiz.why: The main service is on Saturday morning, with the Torah reading.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is the weekly Torah portion?
quiz.why: The parashah is the weekly portion, so the Torah is read in a year.

quiz.q: Which ceremony ends Shabbat?
quiz.why: Havdalah, with wine, a plaited candle and spices, separates Shabbat from the week.

quiz.q: How many categories of work are forbidden on Shabbat according to the rabbis?
quiz.why: The rabbis listed 39 melachot, such as cooking and writing.

quiz.q: Which one of these is placed on the table for the Friday night meal?
quiz.why: Two challah loaves are blessed at the Shabbat meal, remembering the double portion of manna.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is the Oral Law?
quiz.why: The Talmud (Mishnah and Gemara) is the Oral Law. The Tenakh is the Written Law.

quiz.q: What is placed on the doorposts of a Jewish home?
quiz.why: The mezuzah contains the Shema and fulfils Deuteronomy 6:9.

quiz.q: What is the Gemara?
options: The rabbis' commentary on the Mishnah
quiz.why: The Gemara is later rabbinic discussion of the Mishnah. Together they form the Talmud.

quiz.q: Brit Milah takes place on which day after birth?
quiz.why: Genesis 17:12 says a boy is circumcised at eight days old.

quiz.q: Who performs a circumcision?
quiz.why: A mohel is a trained person who performs Brit Milah.

quiz.q: At what age is a boy usually Bar Mitzvah?
quiz.why: Pirkei Avot 5:21 says thirteen is the age for observing the commandments.

quiz.q: Which one of the following differs between Orthodox and Reform Bat Mitzvah?
options: Only Orthodox girls have a party
Reform girls often read from the Torah, while many Orthodox do not in the main service
quiz.why: Reform Bat Mitzvah mirrors the boys' ceremony, while many Orthodox communities mark it differently.

quiz.q: What does the chuppah represent?
quiz.why: The chuppah is the canopy that symbolises the couple's home.

quiz.q: Why does the groom break a glass at a Jewish wedding?
options: To show the marriage is legal
To remember the destruction of the Temple
quiz.why: It recalls the destruction of the Temple and that joy is mixed with sadness.

quiz.q: What is shiva?
quiz.why: Shiva means 'seven': the first seven days of mourning at home.

quiz.q: Which one of these is the yearly anniversary of a death?
quiz.why: Yahrzeit is the anniversary of a death, marked with a candle and Kaddish.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is NOT kosher?
quiz.why: Pigs do not chew the cud, so pork is trefah. Salmon has fins and scales.

quiz.q: Which Torah verse is used as the basis for separating meat and milk?
quiz.why: Exodus 23:19 says 'Do not boil a kid in its mother's milk'.

quiz.q: Which instrument is blown at Rosh Hashanah?
quiz.why: The shofar (ram's horn) is a call to repent.

quiz.q: How long is the fast at Yom Kippur?
quiz.why: The fast is around 25 hours, from before sunset to after nightfall.

quiz.q: What do the bitter herbs (maror) on the Seder plate symbolise?
quiz.why: Maror represents the bitterness of slavery in Egypt.

quiz.q: Why do Jews eat matzah at Pesach?
options: It is the only kosher bread
The Israelites left Egypt in haste with no time for bread to rise
quiz.why: Deuteronomy 16:3 says matzah is 'the bread of affliction' because the Israelites left in haste.

quiz.q: Which Hebrew term means 'house of assembly'?
quiz.why: Bet Knesset (house of assembly) refers to the synagogue as a community meeting place. Bet Din is a Jewish court.

quiz.q: A synagogue runs a Sunday class where children learn Hebrew. Which role of the synagogue does this show?
quiz.why: Bet Midrash means house of study, the synagogue's role in education.

quiz.q: Which one of these is a reason why the synagogue replaced the Temple?
options: The Temple was destroyed in 70 CE
quiz.why: After the Romans destroyed the Temple, synagogue prayer took the place of Temple worship.

quiz.q: In many Reform synagogues, which way does the person leading the service face?
quiz.why: Reform leaders often face the congregation so people can hear and follow; Orthodox leaders face the Ark.

quiz.q: Which word describes the lifting of the open Torah scroll after the reading?
quiz.why: Hagbah means lifting; it lets the congregation see the words of the Torah.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a religious feature of the synagogue building?
quiz.why: A tallit is a prayer shawl worn by a worshipper, not a feature of the building.

quiz.q: Which statement is true of many Orthodox synagogues?
options: An organ is played on Shabbat
quiz.why: Orthodox synagogues have separate seating, with a gallery or mechitzah.

quiz.q: Which reason would a Reform Jew most likely give for mixed seating?
options: Men and women are equal in worship
quiz.why: Reform Judaism stresses equality between men and women.

quiz.q: Which prayers are shared by both Orthodox and Reform services?
quiz.why: Both use the core prayers such as the Shema and the Amidah and read from the Torah.

quiz.q: Which one of the following best describes the Amidah?
quiz.why: The Amidah is the standing prayer, the central prayer of every service.

quiz.q: Whose silent prayer is the model for saying the Amidah quietly?
quiz.why: 1 Samuel 1:13: Hannah's lips moved but her voice was not heard.

quiz.q: How many times a day do Orthodox Jews hold services?
quiz.why: Shacharit, Minchah and Maariv: morning, afternoon and evening.

quiz.q: Which hymn welcomes Shabbat like a bride on Friday evening?
quiz.why: Lekha Dodi ('Come, my beloved') is sung at Kabbalat Shabbat.

quiz.q: What is the reading from the Prophets after the Torah reading called?
quiz.why: The Haftarah is a passage from the Nevi'im (Prophets) linked to the week's Torah portion.

quiz.q: Which of these would you NOT expect in an Orthodox Shabbat service?
quiz.why: Orthodox synagogues do not play instruments on Shabbat.

quiz.q: What do the two challah loaves remember?
quiz.why: God gave a double portion of manna on Fridays so the Israelites did not gather food on Shabbat.

quiz.q: What is said at the end of a meal to thank God?
quiz.why: Birkat Hamazon is the grace after meals.

quiz.q: Which source calls Shabbat a 'delight'?
quiz.why: Isaiah 58:13 says 'if you call the Sabbath a delight'.

quiz.q: Which one of the following do Jews consider to be the written law?
quiz.why: The Tenakh (especially the Torah) is the Written Law; the Talmud is the Oral Law.

quiz.q: Which text lists the 39 categories of work forbidden on Shabbat?
quiz.why: The Talmud (Shabbat 73a, based on the Mishnah) lists the 39 melachot.

quiz.q: Which prayer do many Jews say on waking?
quiz.why: Modeh Ani thanks God for returning the soul in the morning.

quiz.q: Which one of the following events in life is Brit Milah associated with?
quiz.why: Brit Milah is the circumcision of a baby boy on his eighth day.

quiz.q: For whom is a chair set aside at a Brit Milah?
quiz.why: The chair of Elijah: the prophet is seen as guardian of the covenant.

quiz.q: A family gives five silver coins to a kohen 31 days after their first son is born. What is this?
quiz.why: Pidyon Haben is the redemption of the firstborn son.

quiz.q: What does Bat Mitzvah mean?
quiz.why: Bat Mitzvah means 'daughter of the commandment'. Bat Chayil means 'daughter of worth'.

quiz.q: Which source says thirteen is the age for the commandments?
quiz.why: Pirkei Avot 5:21 lists ages for stages of Jewish life, including thirteen for the commandments.

quiz.q: Which of these happens DURING a Bar Mitzvah ceremony?
quiz.why: Reading from the Torah happens in the ceremony; the others are preparation.

quiz.q: What is the Jewish marriage contract called?
quiz.why: The ketubah sets out the husband's duties and protects the wife.

quiz.q: Why does the bride circle the groom seven times in many Orthodox weddings?
options: To show she is building their home together around him
quiz.why: Circling symbolises creating a new family circle and home together; seven recalls the days of creation.

quiz.q: Which of these happens at a Jewish wedding?
quiz.why: The groom breaks a glass to remember the destruction of the Temple.

quiz.q: What do Jews traditionally leave on a grave when they visit?
quiz.why: A stone shows the grave has been visited and the person remembered.

quiz.q: Which verse supports burying the dead quickly?
quiz.why: Deuteronomy 21:23 says the body must be buried the same day.

quiz.q: During which period do mourners sit on low stools and receive visitors at home?
quiz.why: Shiva is the seven days of intense mourning at home.

quiz.q: Which of these could be eaten with a dairy meal in a kosher home?
quiz.why: Fish with fins and scales is pareve, so it can be eaten with dairy; meat and poultry cannot.

quiz.q: Who performs shechitah?
quiz.why: A shochet is trained in kosher slaughter.

quiz.q: Which group would most likely see kashrut as binding on all Jews?
quiz.why: Orthodox Jews see the food laws as God's commandments that must be kept.

quiz.q: Which festival is called Yom HaDin, the Day of Judgement?
quiz.why: Rosh Hashanah is the day God judges the world for the coming year.

quiz.q: Which service begins Yom Kippur?
quiz.why: Kol Nidre is sung on the evening Yom Kippur begins; Neilah closes the day.

quiz.q: What is thrown into flowing water at Tashlich?
quiz.why: Breadcrumbs represent sins being cast away (Micah 7:19). Examiners noted confusion with stones.

quiz.q: What does charoset on the Seder plate represent?
options: The mortar used by the slaves
quiz.why: Charoset is a sweet paste that looks like the mortar the Israelites used to make bricks.

quiz.q: Which book of the Tenakh tells the story of the first Passover?
quiz.why: Exodus 12 describes the Passover lamb, the tenth plague and leaving Egypt.

quiz.q: Who asks the Four Questions at the Seder?
quiz.why: The youngest child asks 'Why is this night different?', so the story is passed on.

truefalse.s: Jews believe God can only hear prayers said in a synagogue.
truefalse.why: Jews believe God is everywhere and hears prayer anywhere; the synagogue matters for communal worship.

truefalse.s: A synagogue has three main roles: prayer, study and assembly.
truefalse.why: Bet Tefillah, Bet Midrash and Bet Knesset.

truefalse.s: Kaddish can be said by a mourner praying alone at home.
truefalse.why: Kaddish needs a minyan of ten, so mourners go to the synagogue to say it.

truefalse.s: Many synagogues run charity and social action projects.
truefalse.why: As a Bet Knesset the synagogue organises community activities such as food bank collections.

truefalse.s: Orthodox and Reform Jews both count women in a minyan.
truefalse.why: Orthodox Jews count only men aged 13 and over; Reform Jews count men and women.

truefalse.s: The Aron Hakodesh is usually on the wall facing Jerusalem.
truefalse.why: So that worshippers facing the Ark also face Jerusalem and the site of the Temple.

truefalse.s: The Ner Tamid is lit only during services.
truefalse.why: It is an ever-burning light that is never allowed to go out, showing God's constant presence.

truefalse.s: Orthodox synagogues usually have an organ for Shabbat services.
truefalse.why: Orthodox worship on Shabbat is unaccompanied; organs are found in many Reform synagogues.

truefalse.s: The yad is used so that the reader does not touch the Torah parchment.
truefalse.why: The scroll is handwritten and holy, so a pointer is used to follow the text.

truefalse.s: A mechitzah separates men and women in Orthodox synagogues.
truefalse.why: It is a screen or barrier, used so worshippers can concentrate on prayer.

truefalse.s: Reform services use only English.
truefalse.why: They use a mix of Hebrew and English (the local language).

truefalse.s: In Reform synagogues women can be rabbis.
truefalse.why: Reform Judaism has ordained women rabbis for decades and counts women in the minyan.

truefalse.s: Orthodox and Reform Jews both read from the Torah scroll in Shabbat services.
truefalse.why: The Torah reading is central in both traditions.

truefalse.s: Orthodox men often wear a kippah and tallit in services.
truefalse.why: Covering the head and wearing a prayer shawl are traditional for men at prayer.

truefalse.s: Orthodox services are usually shorter than Reform ones.
truefalse.why: Orthodox services are usually longer, with more prayers in Hebrew.

truefalse.s: The Amidah is said facing Jerusalem.
truefalse.why: Jews outside Israel face Jerusalem, the site of the Temple, when they pray.

truefalse.s: On Shabbat the Amidah contains all 13 requests.
truefalse.why: On Shabbat the requests are replaced by one blessing for the holiness of the day.

truefalse.s: Kavanah means saying prayers as quickly as possible.
truefalse.why: Kavanah means concentration and sincere intention.

truefalse.s: The rabbis linked the three daily services to the daily offerings in the Temple.
truefalse.why: The Talmud (Berakhot 26b) connects the prayers to the Patriarchs and the Temple offerings.

truefalse.s: Jews may pray in their own words as well as using the siddur.
truefalse.why: Fixed prayers are central, but personal prayer in any language is also valued.

truefalse.s: The whole Torah is read in synagogue over the course of a year.
truefalse.why: It is divided into weekly portions (parashot), finishing at Simchat Torah.

truefalse.s: The main Shabbat service is on Friday morning.
truefalse.why: Shabbat begins on Friday evening; the main service is Saturday morning.

truefalse.s: In many Reform synagogues women can be called up to read from the Torah.
truefalse.why: Reform Judaism gives men and women equal roles in worship.

truefalse.s: The Torah is read from the Aron Hakodesh itself.
truefalse.why: It is kept in the Ark but read from the bimah.

truefalse.s: Shabbat candles are lit after sunset on Friday.
truefalse.why: They are lit shortly before sunset, since lighting a fire is not allowed once Shabbat has begun.

truefalse.s: Havdalah uses wine, spices and a plaited candle.
truefalse.why: These mark the separation between Shabbat and the working week.

truefalse.s: Shabbat may be broken to save a life.
truefalse.why: Pikuach Nefesh overrides Shabbat laws.

truefalse.s: Shabbat is meant to be a sad and serious day.
truefalse.why: It is a joyful day of rest, family, good food and song.

truefalse.s: The Talmud is made up of the Mishnah and the Gemara.
truefalse.why: The Mishnah (c. 200 CE) and the Gemara (later commentary) together form the Talmud.

truefalse.s: The Torah is the third part of the Tenakh.
truefalse.why: The Torah is the first part; then Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).

truefalse.s: Orthodox Jews believe the Oral Law was given to Moses at Sinai.
truefalse.why: They believe it was passed down by word of mouth before being written in the Mishnah and Talmud.

truefalse.s: Jewish prayer can only happen in a synagogue.
truefalse.why: Much prayer happens at home: blessings, Shema, Modeh Ani and private prayer.

truefalse.s: A Torah scroll used in synagogue is printed by machine.
truefalse.why: It is handwritten on parchment by a sofer.

truefalse.s: Brit Milah can take place on Shabbat if it is the eighth day.
truefalse.why: The commandment of the eighth day overrides Shabbat, unless the baby is unwell.

truefalse.s: Jewish babies are baptised in the synagogue.
truefalse.why: Baptism is a Christian practice. Jewish boys have Brit Milah and girls have naming ceremonies.

truefalse.s: Girls in Reform communities may have a Brit Bat or Simchat Bat ceremony.
truefalse.why: These welcome girls into the covenant and community.

truefalse.s: Brit Milah must go ahead on the eighth day even if the baby is ill.
truefalse.why: It is delayed until the baby is healthy because protecting life comes first.

truefalse.s: In Orthodox Judaism a girl becomes Bat Mitzvah at 12.
truefalse.why: Girls are traditionally considered mature a year earlier (Mishnah Niddah 5:6).

truefalse.s: A boy becomes Jewish at his Bar Mitzvah.
truefalse.why: He is already Jewish; he becomes responsible for keeping the mitzvot.

truefalse.s: After his Bar Mitzvah an Orthodox boy counts in the minyan.
truefalse.why: He is now treated as an adult for religious purposes.

truefalse.s: In many Reform synagogues Bar and Bat Mitzvah ceremonies are the same.
truefalse.why: Reform Judaism stresses equality, so girls read from the Torah just like boys.

truefalse.s: Every Orthodox girl reads from the Torah in the main Shabbat service for her Bat Mitzvah.
truefalse.why: In most Orthodox communities women do not read from the Torah in the main service; girls may give a talk or hold a Bat Chayil.

truefalse.s: The chuppah symbolises the couple's new home.
truefalse.why: The canopy open on all sides recalls Abraham's tent and the couple's future home.

truefalse.s: Orthodox synagogues in Britain conduct same-sex weddings.
truefalse.why: Orthodox Judaism does not; Progressive (Reform and Liberal) synagogues do.

truefalse.s: The Seven Blessings thank God for creation, joy and love.
truefalse.why: The Sheva Berakhot praise God for creating humanity, joy, gladness and love.

truefalse.s: Jewish weddings often take place on Shabbat.
truefalse.why: Weddings are not held on Shabbat or major festivals.

truefalse.s: Jewish funerals usually take place within a few days of death, often within 24 hours.
truefalse.why: Quick burial shows respect for the dead (Deuteronomy 21:23).

truefalse.s: The Kaddish prayer is mainly about death and the afterlife.
truefalse.why: It praises God and does not mention death.

truefalse.s: Shiva lasts for thirty days.
truefalse.why: Shiva lasts seven days; sheloshim is thirty days.

truefalse.s: Mourners may tear a garment or wear a torn ribbon (keriah).
truefalse.why: Keriah is a sign of grief, following biblical examples such as Jacob and David.

truefalse.s: Fish counts as meat in Jewish food laws.
truefalse.why: Fish is pareve (neutral) and can be eaten with dairy.

truefalse.s: To be kosher, a land animal must chew the cud and have split hooves.
truefalse.why: Both signs are needed (Leviticus 11:3), which is why the pig is not kosher.

truefalse.s: All Jews keep the dietary laws in the same way.
truefalse.why: Orthodox Jews keep them strictly; Reform and Liberal Jews treat them as a personal choice.

truefalse.s: Kosher meat must have the blood removed.
truefalse.why: The Torah forbids eating blood because 'the life is in the blood' (Leviticus 17:11).

truefalse.s: Shellfish such as prawns are kosher.
truefalse.why: Only water creatures with fins and scales are kosher.

truefalse.s: Judgement is written on Rosh Hashanah and sealed on Yom Kippur.
truefalse.why: This traditional teaching explains why the Ten Days of Awe are for repentance.

truefalse.s: Yom HaDin refers to judgement after death.
truefalse.why: It refers to God's judgement for the coming year at Rosh Hashanah.

truefalse.s: Yom Kippur is a joyful feast day with special meals.
truefalse.why: It is a 25-hour fast spent in prayer and repentance, though it ends with hope of forgiveness.

truefalse.s: Many Jews wear white on Yom Kippur.
truefalse.why: White symbolises purity and forgiveness (Isaiah 1:18).

truefalse.s: The shofar is a ram's horn.
truefalse.why: It recalls the ram sacrificed instead of Isaac and is a call to repent.

truefalse.s: Chametz is leavened food, such as bread made with yeast.
truefalse.why: It is removed from the home before Pesach.

truefalse.s: Pesach remembers the giving of the Torah at Sinai.
truefalse.why: Pesach remembers the Exodus from Egypt; Shavuot remembers the giving of the Torah.

truefalse.s: The Seder is mainly held in the synagogue.
truefalse.why: The Seder is a home-based family meal, though some communities hold communal Seders.

truefalse.s: Elijah's cup is linked to hope for the Messiah.
truefalse.why: Elijah is believed to announce the coming of the Messiah, so a cup is poured and the door opened.
