exam.q: Explain two different ways in which worship in Orthodox and Reform synagogues is different. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One difference is the seating. In Orthodox synagogues men and women sit separately, often with women in a gallery or behind a mechitzah, so that they can focus on God. In Reform synagogues men and women sit together as equals.

Another difference is the language and music. Orthodox services are almost entirely in Hebrew with no instruments on Shabbat, whereas Reform services use Hebrew and English and often have an organ or choir.
points: Seating: separate (Orthodox) versus together (Reform)
Language: Hebrew only versus Hebrew and English
Music: none on Shabbat versus organ or choir
Leadership: only men versus women can be rabbis and read Torah
Minyan: ten men versus ten adults
Frequency: daily versus mainly Shabbat and festivals
Each difference: 1 mark for the point and 1 mark for development

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Jews celebrate Shabbat at home. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is by lighting the Shabbat candles and sharing the Friday night meal. A woman lights two candles shortly before sunset, to welcome Shabbat, and the family then shares Kiddush and challah, which remembers God's creation and the manna.

Another way is by ending Shabbat with Havdalah on Saturday evening. The family uses a plaited candle, wine and spices, and the sweet smell of the spices shows the hope that the sweetness of Shabbat will carry into the week.
points: Candles and Friday evening meal with Kiddush and challah
Havdalah: wine, spice box, plaited candle
Resting from work and avoiding the 39 melachot
Family time, prayer, study of the Torah
Orthodox strictness versus Reform flexibility
Each way: 1 mark for the point and 1 mark for development

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Bar Mitzvah and Bat Mitzvah may be celebrated. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is the Orthodox Bar Mitzvah at 13. The boy reads from the Torah in the synagogue, wears tallit and tefillin for the first time, and is now counted in a minyan, showing he is responsible for the mitzvot.

Another way is the Reform Bat Mitzvah. The girl, at 12 or 13, may read from the Torah and lead the service just like a boy, which shows equality, whereas many Orthodox girls have a celebration with a speech but do not read from the Torah in the main service.
points: Bar Mitzvah at 13: Torah reading, tallit and tefillin, minyan, speech, party
Reform Bat Mitzvah mirrors boys' ceremony (age 12 or 13)
Orthodox Bat Chayil: usually a celebration at 12 without Torah reading in the main service
Different ages and different roles for girls
Each way: 1 mark for the point and 1 mark for development

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Jews mourn the dead. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is shiva, seven days of intense mourning at home after the funeral. Mourners sit on low stools, cover mirrors and do not work, which shows grief and allows the community to comfort them.

Another way is saying Kaddish and marking the yahrzeit. Children say the Kaddish prayer daily for eleven months after a parent dies, and light a candle on each anniversary, to praise God and remember the person.
points: Burial within 24 hours, simple shroud and coffin, Chevra Kadisha
Tearing clothes (keriah) or wearing a black ribbon
Shiva: seven days, low stools, covered mirrors, no work, visits
Sheloshim and avelut (a year for a parent)
Kaddish and yahrzeit candle
Orthodox (burial only) versus Reform (some accept cremation)
Each way: 1 mark for the point and 1 mark for development

exam.q: Explain two different Jewish views about the importance of the dietary laws. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One view is that held by many Orthodox Jews, who believe the dietary laws are commandments from God, so they must be kept strictly. They eat only kosher food and have separate dishes for meat and dairy, because the Torah says so.

Another view is that of many Reform Jews, who believe keeping kosher is a personal choice. Some keep only some of the rules, such as avoiding pork, while others focus on ethical mitzvot like charity, because they see the food laws as less important today.
points: Orthodox: binding commands (Leviticus 11, Deuteronomy 14); strict observance, separate kitchens
Reform: personal choice and informed free will; some keep partly or not at all
Reasons for keeping: obedience, identity, discipline, holiness
Reasons for not keeping: modern life, priority of ethical mitzvot
Each view: 1 mark for the point and 1 mark for development

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Jews celebrate Rosh Hashanah. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is by blowing the shofar in the synagogue. The ram's horn is a wake-up call to repent, so Jews listen carefully to the sounds as they think about their actions in the past year.

Another way is by eating symbolic foods at home. Jews dip apples in honey to show the hope for a sweet new year, and eat round challah to show the cycle of the year.
points: Shofar: call to repentance
Tashlich: casting away sins at water
Synagogue services and prayers of judgement; Ten Days of Awe
Apples and honey, round challah
Orthodox two days, Reform one day
Each way: 1 mark for the point and 1 mark for development

exam.q: Explain two reasons why the synagogue is important for Jews. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One reason is that the synagogue is a place of prayer. Jews believe the Shekhinah is present when ten people pray together, and some prayers need a minyan. Psalm 84:5 says 'Happy are those who dwell in Your house; they will continually praise You', so Jews attend the synagogue to praise God together.

Another reason is that it is a place of study and community. The synagogue is a Bet Midrash where Jews study the Torah and Talmud, and a Bet Knesset where they gather for celebrations such as Bar Mitzvah. Pirkei Avot 3:6 says that when ten sit and study Torah, the Shekhinah is among them, so studying together in the synagogue brings Jews closer to God and each other.
points: House of prayer (Bet Tefillah): communal worship, minyan, Shekhinah
House of study (Bet Midrash): Torah and Talmud study
House of assembly (Bet Knesset): community life, life-cycle events
Holds the Torah scrolls
Source: Psalm 84:5, Isaiah 56:7, Pirkei Avot 3:6
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each reason

exam.q: Explain two features of a synagogue and why they are important. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One feature is the Aron Hakodesh, the Ark where the Torah scrolls are kept. It is the holiest place in the synagogue and represents the Ark of the Covenant, described in Exodus 25:10-22. This means Jews treat the Torah with great respect, for example standing when the Ark is opened.

Another feature is the Ner Tamid, the ever-burning light above the Ark. Leviticus 24:2 says to keep the lamps burning continually. It reminds Jews that God is always present and is a symbol of the menorah in the Temple.
points: Aron Hakodesh: Torah scrolls, Ark of the Covenant (Exodus 25:10-22)
Ner Tamid: God's constant presence (Leviticus 24:2)
Bimah: Torah reading platform (Nehemiah 8:4)
Other features: menorah, Ten Commandments, mechitzah, yad
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each feature

exam.q: Explain two reasons why prayer is important for Jews. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One reason is that prayer is a way of communicating with God and building a relationship. Jews pray three times a day, and Psalm 55:17 says 'Evening, morning and noon I cry out and He hears my voice'. This means prayer gives Jews comfort and strength and helps them feel close to God in daily life.

Another reason is that prayer expresses faith in God as One, through prayers such as the Shema and Amidah. Maimonides said 'prayer without devotion is not prayer', which shows prayer must come from the heart. This means Jews try to concentrate (kavanah) so that their prayers are sincere.
points: Communication with God and closeness (Psalm 55:17)
Prayer is a mitzvah and part of the covenant
Shema and Amidah as central prayers
Kavanah: sincere intention (Maimonides, 1 Samuel 1:13)
Strength, comfort, reflection; group prayer with minyan
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each reason

exam.q: Explain two ways in which the Talmud is important for Jews. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that the Talmud explains how to keep the laws of the Torah. For example, the Torah says not to work on Shabbat, but the Talmud explains what counts as work. This means Jews can follow Torah laws correctly in daily life.

Another way is that the Talmud applies the law to new situations. Rabbi Dov Linzer said 'the Talmud is really about the conversation, and the conversation never ends'. This means Jews today use the Talmud's way of debate to deal with modern questions, which keeps Judaism relevant.
points: Oral Law: Mishnah and Gemara; explains the Torah
Source of halakhah (Jewish law), such as the 39 melachot on Shabbat
Shows rabbis' debates and applies law to new situations
Orthodox: from Sinai; Reform: valued guidance
Source: Rabbi Linzer, Rabbi Steinsaltz, Pirkei Avot
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each way

exam.q: Explain two reasons why Brit Milah is important for Jews. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One reason is that Brit Milah is the sign of the covenant with Abraham. In Genesis 17:10-11 God says 'Every male among you shall be circumcised... and it will be the sign of the covenant'. This means that Jewish parents circumcise their sons to show that the child is part of God's chosen people.

Another reason is that it is a commandment, performed on the eighth day. Genesis 17:12 says 'At eight days old every male shall be circumcised'. This means Jews carry it out even on Shabbat, as a mitzvah, and a celebration follows, to welcome the baby into the Jewish community.
points: Sign of the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:10-11)
A commandment on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12), even on Shabbat
Welcomes the child into the community; naming
Mohel, sandek, Elijah's chair
Unity of Jews through history
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each reason

exam.q: Explain two ways in which Jewish wedding customs show the importance of marriage. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One way is the chuppah, the canopy under which the couple stand. It symbolises their future home together, and the Seven Blessings said beneath it thank God for creation, joy and love. This shows that marriage is seen as holy and a partnership with God.

Another way is the breaking of the glass. It reminds Jews of the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem. This shows that even at a joyful time Jews remember sadness, so marriage must be strong enough to survive hard times. Genesis 2:24 says 'a man leaves his father and mother and clings to his wife', which shows that marriage is a union created by God.
points: Chuppah as the couple's home; Seven Blessings thanking God
Ring: 'according to the law of Moses and Israel'
Ketubah: the husband's duties
Glass broken: remembering the Temple
Marriage fulfils Genesis 1:28 and Genesis 2:24
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each way

exam.q: 'Jews should always worship in the synagogue.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Some key prayers, such as the Kaddish, need a minyan of ten, and Jews believe the Shekhinah is present when people pray together (Pirkei Avot 3:6).
The synagogue holds the Torah scrolls and provides a holy, quiet place with the Ark and Ner Tamid, which helps Jews concentrate.
It is also a place of study and community, so worship there strengthens Jewish identity.
against: God is everywhere, so Jews can pray anywhere. Psalm 55:17 says to pray morning, noon and night, which is not always possible at the synagogue because of work or distance.
Private prayer is valued, as Hannah prayed silently from her heart (1 Samuel 1:13), and women in Orthodox Judaism are not required to attend daily services.
Worship in the home, such as Shabbat candles, blessings and the Seder, is also central to Judaism.
exam.conclusion: Synagogue worship is very important, but the word 'always' is too strong, because Judaism also values prayer at home and God can be reached anywhere.
exam.model:
There are good reasons why Jews should worship in the synagogue. Some prayers, such as the Kaddish, can only be said if there is a minyan of ten adults, and Jews believe the Shekhinah is present when people pray and study together (Pirkei Avot 3:6). The synagogue also contains the Torah scrolls in the Aron Hakodesh, and the Ner Tamid reminds worshippers that God is always present. This creates a holy atmosphere that helps Jews to focus on God. It is also where they study the Talmud and meet as a community, which keeps Jewish identity strong, especially for a minority. This is a strong argument, because the minyan shows that Judaism sees communal prayer as especially valuable.

However, there are strong arguments against the idea that Jews should always worship there. Jews believe God is everywhere, so prayer can happen anywhere. Psalm 55:17 says to pray evening, morning and noon, but it is often not possible to get to a synagogue three times a day because of work or travel. Private prayer is also valued: in 1 Samuel 1:13, Hannah prayed silently in her heart and God answered. Many Reform Jews attend mainly on Shabbat and festivals, and women in Orthodox Judaism are not required to attend daily services. In addition, much of Jewish worship, such as lighting Shabbat candles, saying Kiddush and holding the Seder, takes place at home. This is also a strong argument, because it shows that Jewish worship is not limited to a building.

In conclusion, I believe that synagogue worship is very important, especially for communal prayer, but 'always' is too strong. Jewish teaching allows prayer anywhere, and home worship is central. The best answer is that Jews should worship in the synagogue when they can, particularly on Shabbat and festivals, but not only there.

exam.q: 'Keeping Shabbat is the most important way of practising Judaism.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Shabbat is one of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:8) and a sign of the covenant (Exodus 31:16-17), so it is a direct command from God.
It happens every week, shaping family life, prayer and rest, so it keeps Jews close to God and each other.
Shabbat remembers creation and the Exodus, and the rabbis said that if all Jews kept two Shabbats the Messiah would come.
against: Other practices are also commanded, such as keeping kosher food laws, praying daily and Brit Milah, which is the sign of the covenant with Abraham.
Some festivals, such as Yom Kippur, are called the holiest day of the year.
Reform Jews see ethical mitzvot like justice and charity as more important than ritual observance such as the rules of Shabbat.
exam.conclusion: Shabbat is among the most important practices because it happens weekly and is in the Ten Commandments, but Jews hold different views on what matters most, so it is not clearly the single most important.
exam.model:
There are strong reasons to say that keeping Shabbat is the most important way of practising Judaism. It is one of the Ten Commandments, where Exodus 20:8 says to 'remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy', and Exodus 31:16-17 calls it a lasting sign of the covenant. It happens every week, and it shapes Jewish life through prayer in the synagogue, the Friday night meal, rest and family time. Shabbat remembers both creation and the Exodus, so it brings together key Jewish beliefs. Isaiah 58:13 calls it a delight, which shows it is a joy as well as a duty. This is a convincing argument, because few other practices are done so regularly and by so many Jews.

However, there are also strong arguments against. Other practices are also commanded by God. Brit Milah is the sign of the covenant with Abraham and keeping kosher is an everyday commitment. Yom Kippur is often called the holiest day of the Jewish year, because it is the day of atonement when Jews seek forgiveness. Reform Jews might argue that ethical mitzvot, such as justice and charity, are more important than ritual practices, and many Reform Jews keep Shabbat less strictly. This is a strong argument because Jews hold differing views on which practices matter most.

In conclusion, I believe that Shabbat is one of the most important practices, as it is a commandment, is weekly and affects the whole family. However, I do not think it is clearly the most important, because Orthodox and Reform Jews rank the practices differently and the Torah gives many commands. A balanced judgement is that Shabbat is central, but no single practice can be said to be the most important for all Jews.

exam.q: 'Dietary laws are no longer important for Jews today.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Many Reform Jews see kashrut as a personal choice and focus instead on ethical mitzvot such as justice and charity (Micah 6:8).
Some argue the laws were for health and hygiene in ancient times, which modern food safety has replaced.
Keeping kosher is difficult in a non-Jewish society, with limited kosher food and cost, so many Jews keep only partly or not at all.
against: Orthodox Jews believe the laws are God's commandments (Leviticus 11, Deuteronomy 14), so they remain binding for all time.
Keeping kosher shows obedience, self-discipline and holiness, and reminds Jews of God at every meal.
It unites Jews around the world and strengthens Jewish identity, so many non-Orthodox Jews still keep some rules.
exam.conclusion: The dietary laws are less important for some Reform Jews, but for Orthodox Jews and for many others they remain a key way to show obedience and identity, so the statement is too broad.
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that dietary laws are no longer important. Many Reform Jews see keeping kosher as a personal choice and believe that ethical mitzvot, such as those in Micah 6:8, 'do justice, love kindness and walk humbly', matter more than ritual rules. Some say the food laws were created for health in ancient times, which is no longer needed with modern food safety. Also, it can be hard and expensive to keep kosher in Britain, where kosher food is not always available, so some Jews keep only some of the rules, such as avoiding pork. This is a reasonable argument, as it explains why many Jews today do not keep all the rules.

However, there are strong arguments against this statement. Orthodox Jews believe that the laws in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 are commandments from God, given to Moses, and so they are binding for all time. Rules such as separating milk and meat (Exodus 23:19) are followed strictly in their homes with separate dishes and sometimes two kitchens. Keeping kosher shows obedience to God, helps develop self-discipline and reminds Jews of God at every meal. It also unites Jews across the world and helps them to keep their identity as a minority. Even many Reform Jews keep some rules for this reason. This is a convincing argument, because it shows that the laws still have deep meaning for many Jews.

In conclusion, I think the statement is not convincing as a general claim. The dietary laws are less important to some Reform Jews, but for Orthodox Jews and for many others they are a key part of obedience to God and Jewish identity. The statement would be more accurate if it said 'for some Jews'.

exam.q: 'Yom Kippur is the most important day in the Jewish year.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Yom Kippur is the Day of Atonement, the holiest day. Leviticus 16:29-30 says atonement will be made to cleanse Jews of sin.
It is the day God seals judgement for the year, so Jews fast, repent and ask forgiveness. Many Jews who do not keep other practices fast and attend synagogue.
It strengthens the relationship with God and with other people through reconciliation, which affects how Jews live afterwards.
against: Shabbat happens weekly and is one of the Ten Commandments, so it shapes Jewish life more often.
Pesach is celebrated by the most Jewish families and tells the story of how God freed the Jews, which is the foundation of Jewish identity.
Rosh Hashanah begins the Ten Days of Awe and is the day of judgement, so it is the start of the process that Yom Kippur completes.
exam.conclusion: Yom Kippur is the holiest day and can claim to be the most important, but because Shabbat and Pesach are also central to the covenant and Jewish identity, no single day is clearly the most important for all Jews.
exam.model:
There is a strong case that Yom Kippur is the most important day in the Jewish year. It is called the Day of Atonement and is the holiest day. Leviticus 16:29-30 says that on this day atonement is made to cleanse Jews of their sins. Jews believe that God seals His judgement for the year, so they fast for 25 hours, spend the day in the synagogue and confess their sins. Many Jews who do not keep other practices still fast on Yom Kippur. It is a chance to be reconciled with God, which Jews believe affects their lives and their future. This is a convincing argument, as the day deals with the most important question for believers: how to be forgiven.

However, there are strong arguments against. Shabbat happens every week and is one of the Ten Commandments, so for many Jews it shapes life more often than Yom Kippur. Pesach is celebrated by many Jewish families around the Seder table and remembers the Exodus, when God freed the Israelites, which is the foundation of Jewish identity and the covenant. Rosh Hashanah is also the day of judgement and starts the Ten Days of Awe, so Yom Kippur only completes the process that begins there. This is also a strong argument, because it shows Jewish festivals are connected and each is important.

In conclusion, I think Yom Kippur has a good claim to be the most important day because of its holiness and focus on forgiveness. However, the statement is too strong, as Shabbat and Pesach are also at the heart of the covenant and Jewish identity, and different Jews give different answers. The best judgement is that Yom Kippur is the most solemn and spiritually significant day, but not the only most important one.

exam.q: 'Bat Mitzvah should be celebrated in exactly the same way as Bar Mitzvah.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Reform Jews believe men and women are equal before God, so girls should read from the Torah and lead the service just as boys do. For them an identical ceremony expresses full equality.
Girls become responsible for the mitzvot as boys do, so they should have the same recognition and public ceremony.
Equal ceremonies show that girls' Jewish education and contribution are valued by the community.
against: Orthodox Jews believe men and women have different religious roles, so women are not called to read the Torah in the main service. Some Orthodox rabbis see a formal Bat Mitzvah as unnecessary, as girls already take on the mitzvot at 12 and are not counted in a minyan.
Girls usually celebrate at 12 and boys at 13, so the ceremonies are not exactly the same by tradition.
Boys wear tallit and tefillin and join the minyan, which girls do not do in Orthodox practice.
exam.conclusion: For Reform Jews equality means the ceremonies should be the same, but for Orthodox Jews tradition gives different roles, so the answer depends on the tradition, though equal recognition is persuasive in modern society.
exam.model:
Many Reform Jews would agree with this statement. They believe men and women are equal before God, so girls should have the same ceremony as boys, including reading from the Torah and leading parts of the service. The Mishnah (Niddah 5:6) treats a girl as responsible for her own vows from the age of 12, so she takes on the mitzvot just as a boy does at 13. Girls take on responsibility for the mitzvot as boys do, so they should receive the same recognition. In many Reform synagogues the ceremonies are indeed identical, with a Torah reading, a speech and a celebration. This is a strong argument, because it matches modern values and recognises the girl's religious maturity.

However, Orthodox Jews would disagree. They believe men and women have different religious roles, so women are not called to read from the Torah in the main service or count in a minyan. In the past, Bat Mitzvah did not exist, because girls were thought to learn their faith at home, and some Orthodox rabbis still consider it unnecessary. Also, girls traditionally celebrate at 12 and boys at 13, and only boys wear tefillin and a tallit for the first time. Many Orthodox communities hold a Bat Chayil celebration, with a speech and a meal, that honours the girl in a different way. This is a strong argument because it follows long-standing tradition and sees difference as respect rather than inequality.

In conclusion, the answer depends on the tradition. For Reform Jews, equality is a fundamental belief, so the ceremonies should be the same. For Orthodox Jews, the ceremonies are different because roles are different. I think the argument for equal recognition is more persuasive in modern society, but the strongest answer recognises that both approaches reflect sincere beliefs about how to follow God's law.

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which a synagogue is used by Jews. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is as a house of prayer (Bet Tefillah). Jews gather for daily, Shabbat and festival services, and prayers such as Kaddish and the Torah reading can only take place when a minyan of ten is present.

A different way is as a house of study (Bet Midrash). Children attend cheder to learn Hebrew and about Judaism so they can follow the prayers, and adults meet to study the Torah and Talmud, often with the rabbi.
points: Prayer: daily and Shabbat services, minyan, Torah reading (Bet Tefillah)
Study: cheder, Hebrew classes, adult Torah and Talmud study, library (Bet Midrash)
Community: social events, youth clubs, charity, kosher meals (Bet Knesset)
Life-cycle ceremonies: baby naming, Bar/Bat Mitzvah, weddings
Festivals: Yom Kippur services, Simchat Torah, communal Seders
Each way: 1 mark simple, 2 marks detailed; the two ways must be different

exam.q: Explain two different practices associated with the Torah scrolls in the synagogue. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One practice is that the congregation stands when the Aron Hakodesh is opened and the scroll is taken out. This shows respect, because the Torah is believed to be God's word and is the holiest object in the synagogue.

A different practice is that the scroll is read from the bimah using a yad (pointer). The reader does not touch the parchment with their hand because the scroll is handwritten and holy, and afterwards the open scroll is lifted up (hagbah) so everyone can see the words.
points: Standing when the Ark is opened; opening the Ark is an honour
Procession round the synagogue; touching and kissing with tallit or siddur (Ezekiel 3:3)
Reading from the bimah with a yad; members called up for an aliyah
Hagbah: lifting the scroll; dressing it in its mantle and crown
Kept in the Aron Hakodesh behind the parochet, facing Jerusalem
Each way: 1 mark simple, 2 marks detailed; practices must be different

exam.q: 'The bimah is the most important feature of the synagogue.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: The Torah is read from the bimah, so it is where God's word is heard by the community, the high point of the Shabbat service (compare Ezra reading the law from a platform, Nehemiah 8:4).
In Orthodox synagogues it stands in the centre, showing the Torah is at the heart of the community and meant for the whole world.
Bar and Bat Mitzvah readings and aliyot happen there, so key moments in Jewish life take place on the bimah.
against: The Aron Hakodesh holds the Torah scrolls, faces Jerusalem and recalls the Ark of the Covenant; the bimah is only used when the scrolls are taken from the Ark.
The Ner Tamid is a constant reminder of God's presence and recalls the lamp in the Tabernacle (Exodus 27:20).
Jewish teaching says it is the Torah and the community (the minyan) that matter, not any piece of furniture; a synagogue can work in any room.
exam.conclusion: The bimah is important because the Torah is read there, but its value comes from the Torah kept in the Ark, so the Aron Hakodesh (or the Torah itself) is more important.
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that the bimah is the most important feature. It is the raised platform from which the Torah is read, and the Torah reading is the high point of the Shabbat morning service. This follows an ancient practice: Nehemiah 8:4 describes Ezra standing on a wooden platform to read the law to all the people. In Orthodox synagogues the bimah is often in the centre, which shows that the Torah is at the heart of the community and should be heard by everyone. Many of the most important moments in a Jew's life, such as reading from the Torah at a Bar or Bat Mitzvah, happen on the bimah. This is a strong argument, because the Torah is meant to be read and lived, not just stored.

However, others would argue that the Aron Hakodesh is more important. It holds the Torah scrolls, the holiest objects in Judaism, and it recalls the Ark of the Covenant in the Holy of Holies. It is placed on the wall facing Jerusalem, so it shows the direction of prayer, and the whole congregation stands when it is opened. The bimah is only used when the scrolls are brought out of the Ark. Some might choose the Ner Tamid, which reminds Jews of God's constant presence and recalls the lamp kept burning in the Tabernacle (Exodus 27:20). Others would say no feature is most important, because a minyan can pray anywhere and the building is not holy in itself.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement. The bimah has an important purpose, but its importance depends on the Torah, which is kept in the Aron Hakodesh. Since the Torah scrolls are what give both features their meaning, I think the Ark, as the place where the Torah is kept, is the most important feature, while recognising that Jews value each feature for its role in worship.

exam.q: Explain two ways in which Jews worship together in the synagogue. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One way is by reading from the Torah. On Shabbat the scroll is taken from the Ark and a portion is read from the bimah, with members called up for an aliyah to say blessings. This follows Deuteronomy 31:12, which commands the people to gather so they can hear and learn the Torah. This means the community hears God's word together every week.

Another way is by saying set prayers with a minyan, such as the Shema and the Amidah. In Orthodox synagogues these are said in Hebrew with men and women seated separately, while Reform synagogues use Hebrew and English and may use music. The Talmud (Berakhot 6a) teaches that when ten people pray together the divine presence is with them, so Jews value praying as a community.
points: Torah reading from the bimah, aliyah, Haftarah (Deuteronomy 31:12, Nehemiah 8)
Set prayers: Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), Amidah; need for a minyan (Berakhot 6a)
Singing led by chazan; Reform use of organ or choir (Psalm 150)
Sermon by rabbi; Kiddush after the service
Orthodox and Reform differences in language, seating and leadership
Marks: 2 per developed way, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: 'Synagogue services should be in English, not Hebrew.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Prayer needs kavanah (sincere concentration); Maimonides taught prayer without devotion is not prayer, which is hard if people do not understand the words.
Deuteronomy 31:12 says the people should gather so they 'may hear and learn': understanding is part of worship. The Mishnah allows the Shema and Amidah to be said in any language.
Many British Jews do not read Hebrew well; English helps young people and converts feel included, which is why Reform services use a lot of English.
against: Hebrew is the holy language of the Torah; reading God's words in the original keeps their exact meaning.
Hebrew unites Jews across the world and through history: a Jew can join a service anywhere and recognise the prayers.
Learning Hebrew for Bar and Bat Mitzvah keeps Jewish identity strong; most Reform services still keep key prayers like the Shema in Hebrew, and the Torah is always read in Hebrew.
exam.conclusion: A mix may be best: understanding matters for kavanah, but Hebrew links Jews to the Torah and each other, so replacing it completely would lose something important.
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that services should be in English. Prayer in Judaism must be said with kavanah, sincere concentration, and Maimonides taught that prayer without devotion is not really prayer. It is hard to concentrate on words you do not understand, and many Jews in Britain do not read Hebrew fluently. Deuteronomy 31:12 commands the people to gather so that they 'may hear and learn', suggesting understanding is part of worship, and the Mishnah allows the Shema and the Amidah to be said in any language. This is why Reform synagogues use a lot of English, which also helps children, converts and visitors feel included. This is a strong argument, because worship that people do not understand risks becoming empty words.

However, many Jews, especially Orthodox Jews, would disagree. Hebrew is the holy language in which the Torah was given, so reading and praying in it keeps the exact meaning of God's words, which can be lost in translation. Hebrew also unites Jews across the world and across history: a Jew from Manchester can walk into a synagogue in Jerusalem or New York and join in. Learning Hebrew for a Bar or Bat Mitzvah connects young people to their tradition and identity. Even Reform services keep key prayers like the Shema in Hebrew, and the Torah scroll is always read in Hebrew. This is a convincing argument, because Hebrew is part of what makes Jewish worship Jewish.

In conclusion, I do not fully agree. Understanding is important, so English translations and some English prayers help worshippers pray with kavanah. But replacing Hebrew completely would weaken the link to the Torah and to Jews everywhere. A mix, with translations available, seems the most balanced approach, which is what many British synagogues already do in different ways.

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Jews pray. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is praying together in the synagogue with a minyan. Orthodox men aim to attend the three daily services, where the Amidah is said silently and then repeated aloud by the leader, and Kaddish can be said.

A different way is private prayer at home. Jews say the Modeh Ani prayer on waking, the Shema before going to sleep and blessings before and after food, and they can also speak to God in their own words in any language.
points: Communal prayer with a minyan in synagogue: three daily services, repetition of the Amidah
Private prayer at home: Modeh Ani, bedtime Shema, personal prayer
Standing silent Amidah versus the Shema said aloud as a declaration
Use of tallit and tefillin (weekday mornings) by Orthodox men
Orthodox in Hebrew versus Reform in Hebrew and English
Each way: 1 mark simple, 2 marks detailed; ways must be different

exam.q: 'The Amidah is the most important Jewish prayer.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: It is called HaTefillah, 'the Prayer', and is the centre of every service, said three times a day.
It covers every kind of prayer: praise, requests (wisdom, healing, forgiveness, the Messiah, Jerusalem) and thanks, so it expresses the whole of Jewish faith.
It replaces the Temple offerings (Berakhot 26b; Hosea 14:2) and is said standing as before a king, showing its special status.
against: The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is a command in the Torah itself and declares the most basic belief, that God is One; it is said morning and night and traditionally before death.
Kaddish has great importance for mourners and the community, and personal prayer from the heart may matter more than any fixed text: Maimonides said prayer without devotion is not prayer.
Reform Jews have changed parts of the Amidah, so its exact form is not agreed by all Jews.
exam.conclusion: The Amidah is the central prayer of worship, but the Shema is the central declaration of belief, so each is most important in a different way.
exam.model:
Many Jews would agree that the Amidah is the most important prayer. The rabbis call it HaTefillah, 'the Prayer', because it is the centre of every service, said three times a day. It contains every type of prayer: blessings of praise, requests for wisdom, forgiveness, healing, justice and the coming of the Messiah, and finally thanks and a prayer for peace. The Talmud (Berakhot 26b) links the daily services to the offerings in the Temple, and since the Temple was destroyed prayer has replaced sacrifice, as Hosea 14:2 says, 'we will offer the words of our lips'. Worshippers stand, face Jerusalem and bow as if before a king, which shows how seriously it is taken. This is a strong argument because no other prayer covers so much of Jewish belief and life.

However, others would say the Shema is more important. Unlike the Amidah, the Shema is a passage from the Torah itself (Deuteronomy 6:4-9), and it declares the most basic Jewish belief, that God is One. It is said morning and night, placed in the mezuzah and tefillin, and traditionally said as a Jew's last words. Some would also point to Kaddish, which mourners say to praise God even in grief. Others argue that no fixed prayer is most important, because prayer must have kavanah: Maimonides taught that prayer without devotion is not prayer, so a sincere private prayer could matter more. Also, Reform prayer books have changed parts of the Amidah, showing not all Jews agree on its exact words.

In conclusion, I think the Amidah is the most important prayer of worship, because it is the heart of every service and includes all kinds of prayer. However, the Shema is the most important statement of belief. Since they do different jobs, it is fairer to say both are central, and both only have value when said with kavanah.

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Orthodox and Reform Jews may celebrate Shabbat in the synagogue. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One difference is in music and language. In Orthodox synagogues the service is mostly in Hebrew and is sung without instruments, because playing music counts as work on Shabbat; in many Reform synagogues English is used alongside Hebrew and an organ or choir may accompany the singing.

Another difference is who takes part. In Orthodox synagogues only men are called up to read from the Torah and men and women sit separately, while in Reform synagogues women can read from the Torah, lead the service and sit with their families, because Reform Judaism stresses equality.
points: Language: mostly Hebrew (Orthodox) versus Hebrew and English (Reform)
Music: unaccompanied singing (Orthodox) versus organ or choir (Reform)
Roles: only men read Torah (Orthodox) versus women read and lead (Reform)
Seating: separate versus mixed
Travel: walking (Orthodox) versus some driving (Reform); length of service
Each way: 1 mark simple, 2 marks detailed; must be different

exam.q: Explain two ways in which the Torah is honoured during the Shabbat service. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One way is the procession. The Ark is opened, the congregation stands, and the scroll is carried round the synagogue to the bimah while people sing. Worshippers touch it with their tallit fringes or prayer book and kiss them, as the prophet Ezekiel said God's scroll 'tasted as sweet as honey' (Ezekiel 3:3). This shows Jews love the Torah as God's precious gift.

Another way is how it is read. Members of the community are called up for an aliyah to say blessings before and after each section, and the reader uses a yad so the parchment is not touched. Afterwards the scroll is lifted high so everyone can see the words. This follows Ezra, who read the law to the people from a platform while they stood (Nehemiah 8:4-5), showing that the Torah is God's word for the whole community.
points: Standing when the Ark is opened; procession; touching and kissing (Ezekiel 3:3)
Aliyah blessings; reading with a yad; hagbah lifting the scroll
Read from the raised bimah so all can hear (Nehemiah 8:4-5)
Weekly parashah so the whole Torah is read each year (Joshua 1:8: recite it day and night)
Sermon explaining the portion; Bar/Bat Mitzvah reading
Marks: 2 per developed way, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: 'Going to the synagogue is the most important part of keeping Shabbat.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: The Torah is read in the synagogue each Shabbat, so the community hears God's word together; this only happens with a minyan.
Communal prayer brings the Shekhinah (Berakhot 6a) and makes Shabbat feel different from the rest of the week.
It strengthens the community: Kiddush after the service, Bar and Bat Mitzvah, and support for those who live alone.
against: Shabbat began as a day of rest at home: 'Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy' (Exodus 20:8) is about rest from work for the whole household, which happens in the home.
The home rituals (candles, Kiddush, challah, family meal, Havdalah) are where families pass on traditions, and many say the Jewish home is a small sanctuary.
Orthodox women are not required to attend services; some Jews cannot attend due to illness or distance, yet keep Shabbat fully. Not working (the 39 melachot) is the core command.
exam.conclusion: Synagogue worship is a vital part of Shabbat, but rest and home life are the core of the commandment, so the home is at least equally important.
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that going to the synagogue is the most important part of Shabbat. The Torah is read publicly every Shabbat morning, and this can only happen with a minyan, so the community hears God's word together and every synagogue in the world reads the same portion. The Talmud (Berakhot 6a) teaches that the divine presence is with ten who pray together, so communal worship helps Jews feel close to God. The synagogue is also where young people celebrate their Bar or Bat Mitzvah, and where the Kiddush after the service brings the community together. This is a strong argument because Shabbat is a sign of the covenant with the whole people, not just individuals.

However, there are strong reasons to disagree. The commandment says 'Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy. Six days you shall labour... but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God' (Exodus 20:8-10), which is mainly about rest from work, and it includes the whole household. Much of Shabbat happens in the home: lighting candles, Kiddush over wine, blessing the challah and children, a family meal with songs, and Havdalah at the end. These rituals pass on Jewish traditions to children. In Orthodox Judaism women are not obliged to attend synagogue services, and people who are ill or live far from a synagogue can still keep Shabbat fully by resting and celebrating at home. This is a convincing argument because the heart of Shabbat is rest and holiness, which can happen anywhere.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement. Synagogue worship is an important part of Shabbat, especially hearing the Torah, but the core of the commandment is rest and making the day holy, which is centred on the home. Most Jews would see the home and the synagogue as working together to make Shabbat special.

exam.q: Explain two reasons why Shabbat is important for Jews. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One reason is that keeping Shabbat is commanded by God and remembers creation. Exodus 20:8-11 says 'Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy' and explains that God rested on the seventh day after creating the world. This means Jews stop work from Friday sunset to Saturday night to copy God's rest and to thank God as Creator.

Another reason is that Shabbat is the sign of the covenant between God and the Jewish people. Exodus 31:16 says the Israelites shall keep the Sabbath 'as a lasting covenant'. This means that by lighting candles, saying Kiddush and resting each week, Jews show their special relationship with God and pass this identity on to their children.
points: Commanded in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:8-11; Deuteronomy 5:12)
Remembers creation (Genesis 2:2-3) and freedom from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15)
Sign of the covenant (Exodus 31:16-17)
Time for family, rest, prayer and study; 'a delight' (Isaiah 58:13)
Unites Jews and preserves identity ('Shabbat has kept the Jews')
Marks: 2 per developed reason, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Jews worship in the home. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is through daily prayers and blessings. Many Jews say Modeh Ani on waking and the Shema before sleeping, and they say blessings before and after food to thank God for providing it.

A different way is through Shabbat and festival rituals at the table. On Friday night the family lights candles, says Kiddush over wine and blesses the challah, and at Pesach the family holds the Seder, so the home becomes a 'small sanctuary' where children learn their faith.
points: Daily prayers: Modeh Ani, bedtime Shema, private prayer
Blessings over food and Birkat Hamazon
Mezuzah on doorposts, touched when passing
Shabbat and festival rituals: candles, Kiddush, Seder, Havdalah
Torah study at home; teaching children (Deuteronomy 6:7)
Each way: 1 mark simple, 2 marks detailed; ways must be different

exam.q: 'The Talmud is just as important as the Torah for Jews today.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Orthodox Jews believe the Oral Law was given to Moses at Sinai with the Written Law (Pirkei Avot 1:1), so both come from God.
The Torah cannot be kept without the Talmud: it explains the 39 melachot, how to make tefillin and how to keep kashrut.
The Talmud applies the law to new situations and its debates are studied daily (Daf Yomi); Steinsaltz called it the 'central pillar' of Judaism.
against: The Torah is the direct word of God, written in the Sefer Torah, kept in the Ark and read in every synagogue; the Talmud is the words of rabbis about it.
The Talmud depends on the Torah: it is commentary, so it cannot be equal to its source.
Many Reform Jews see the Talmud as valuable human guidance, not binding law, while the Torah's ethical teaching stays central.
exam.conclusion: The Torah has the higher status as God's word, but for many Jews, especially Orthodox, it can only be lived out through the Talmud, so in practice both are essential.
exam.model:
Many Jews, especially Orthodox Jews, would agree with this statement. They believe that when Moses received the Written Torah at Sinai he also received the Oral Torah, which was passed down by word of mouth and later written as the Mishnah and Gemara. Pirkei Avot 1:1 traces this chain from Moses to Joshua and onwards. In practice the Torah cannot be kept without the Talmud. The Torah says not to work on Shabbat, but it is the Talmud that lists the 39 melachot. The Torah says to bind God's words on your hand, but the Talmud explains how to make and wear tefillin. The Talmud also shows rabbis debating, which helps Jews apply the law to new situations. Rabbi Adin Steinsaltz called it the 'central pillar' of Judaism, and many Jews study it every day through Daf Yomi. This is a strong argument, because daily Jewish life depends on it.

However, others would argue the Torah is more important. It is believed to be the direct word of God, handwritten by a scribe on a scroll that is kept in the Aron Hakodesh, carried in procession and read in every synagogue. The Talmud is a record of what rabbis said about the Torah, so it depends on the Torah and cannot be greater than its source. Many Reform Jews see the Talmud as wise human guidance that can be reinterpreted, while the Torah, especially its ethical teaching, remains central. This is a convincing argument because the Talmud itself constantly quotes the Torah as its authority.

In conclusion, I think the Torah has the higher status, because it is God's word and the source of everything else. However, for many Jews, especially Orthodox Jews, the Torah can only be lived through the Talmud's explanations, so in daily practice they are both essential, even if they are not exactly equal.

exam.q: Explain two different ceremonies associated with the birth of a Jewish child. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One ceremony is Brit Milah, for baby boys on the eighth day after birth. A trained mohel circumcises the baby while he is held by the sandek, the father thanks God for bringing his son into the covenant of Abraham, and the boy is given his Hebrew name.

A different ceremony is the naming of a baby girl. In Orthodox communities the father is called up to the Torah on Shabbat and the girl's name is announced with a prayer for mother and baby, while many Reform families hold a Simchat Bat at any time, where both parents say prayers and family and friends celebrate.
points: Brit Milah: eighth day, mohel, sandek, chair of Elijah, Hebrew name, sign of covenant
Girls: naming in synagogue on Shabbat (Orthodox); Simchat Bat or Brit Bat (Reform)
Pidyon Haben for a firstborn son on day 31
Shalom Zachar on the first Friday night after a boy's birth
Whispering the Shema to a newborn
Each way: 1 mark simple, 2 marks detailed; ceremonies must be different

exam.q: 'Brit Milah is the most important Jewish ceremony.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: It is commanded directly by God in the Torah (Genesis 17:10-12) as the sign of the covenant with Abraham, carried out on the eighth day even on Shabbat.
It marks a Jewish boy permanently as part of the covenant, and is kept even by many Jews who keep few other practices.
It begins Jewish life; the blessing hopes the child will enter Torah, marriage and good deeds, so it opens the way to all later ceremonies.
against: It applies only to boys, so it cannot be the most important ceremony for all Jews; girls' ceremonies and Bat Mitzvah matter equally to many Reform Jews.
Bar and Bat Mitzvah may be more important because the young person chooses to accept the mitzvot for themselves (Pirkei Avot 5:21), while a baby has no choice.
Weekly Shabbat or yearly Yom Kippur shape faith more often; marriage is a mitzvah (Genesis 1:28) that builds Jewish families, and mourning rituals honour life and God.
exam.conclusion: Brit Milah is the most important ceremony for many Jewish families because it is a direct command and the sign of the covenant, but because it applies only to boys and is not chosen, others see Bar/Bat Mitzvah or weekly practices as equally important.
exam.model:
Many Jews would agree that Brit Milah is the most important ceremony. It is commanded directly by God in the Torah: 'Every male among you shall be circumcised... at eight days old' (Genesis 17:10-12). It is the sign of the covenant between God and Abraham, so it marks a Jewish boy as part of God's people for life. It is so important that it takes place on the eighth day even if that day is Shabbat or Yom Kippur. Many Jews who do not keep other mitzvot still have their sons circumcised, which shows how deeply it is connected to Jewish identity. The blessing said at the ceremony hopes the boy will enter 'into Torah, into marriage and into good deeds', so it is the start of every other stage of Jewish life. This is a strong argument because it comes straight from the covenant with Abraham.

However, others would disagree. Brit Milah only applies to boys, so it cannot be the most important ceremony for every Jew. Many Reform Jews would point to ceremonies such as Brit Bat and Bat Mitzvah to show girls are equally part of the covenant. A baby has no say in Brit Milah, whereas at a Bar or Bat Mitzvah a young person personally takes on the mitzvot, which Pirkei Avot 5:21 links to the age of thirteen. Marriage could also be seen as more important, because it fulfils the mitzvah to 'be fruitful and multiply' (Genesis 1:28) and creates the Jewish home where faith is passed on. This is a convincing argument because it shows that different ceremonies matter at different points in life.

In conclusion, I think Brit Milah is the most important ceremony in one sense, because it is a direct command from God and the sign of the covenant. However, as it only applies to boys and is not chosen by the person, I would say it is one of several equally important stages, with Bar and Bat Mitzvah and marriage also central to Jewish life.

exam.q: Explain two reasons why Bar Mitzvah is important for Jews. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One reason is that it marks the point when a boy becomes responsible for keeping the mitzvot himself. Pirkei Avot 5:21 teaches that thirteen is the age for the commandments. This means that from now on he must fast on Yom Kippur and keep the laws, and his father thanks God that he is no longer responsible for his son's wrongdoing.

Another reason is that it shows the young person taking on the covenant and joining the adult community. He reads from the Torah in front of the congregation for the first time, wears a tallit and is counted in the minyan. The Torah was given to the whole people at Sinai, when they said 'All that the Lord has spoken we will do' (Exodus 24:7), so each Bar Mitzvah is like a young Jew making that promise personally.
points: Responsibility for the mitzvot at 13 (Pirkei Avot 5:21); father's blessing
Joining the adult community: counted in minyan, called up for aliyah
Personally accepting the covenant made at Sinai (Exodus 24:7)
Continuing Jewish identity and tradition; study of Torah and Hebrew
Celebration with family and community; wearing tallit and tefillin
Marks: 2 per developed reason, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Jewish weddings may be celebrated. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is the Orthodox tradition where the bride circles the groom seven times under the chuppah and only the groom gives a ring, saying 'You are consecrated to me by this ring according to the law of Moses and Israel'. Afterwards men and women often dance separately.

A different way is in Reform or Liberal synagogues, where the ceremony is more equal. Both partners may give rings and make the declaration to each other, circling may be shared or left out, and same-sex couples can also marry.
points: Orthodox: bride circles seven times, groom gives ring, separate dancing, fasting beforehand
Reform/Progressive: exchange of rings, equal declarations, same-sex weddings possible
Ceremony symbols: chuppah (home), ketubah, Seven Blessings, breaking glass (Temple), yichud
Before: aufruf, bedeken (veiling)
After: Sheva Berakhot week of celebration (Orthodox)
Each way: 1 mark simple, 2 marks detailed; ways must be different

exam.q: 'Marriage is the most important stage in Jewish life.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Marriage fulfils the first mitzvah in the Torah, 'Be fruitful and multiply' (Genesis 1:28), and God said 'It is not good for the man to be alone' (Genesis 2:18).
The Jewish home is where the faith is passed on: Shabbat, festivals and kashrut are mainly kept at home, so marriage protects the future of Judaism.
The rabbis call marriage kiddushin (holiness), and the Talmud says a man without a wife lives without joy or blessing (Yevamot 62b).
against: Brit Milah is a direct command and the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17), so it could be more important.
Bar and Bat Mitzvah is when a Jew personally accepts the mitzvot; this matters for every Jew, married or not.
Not everyone marries, and a single person can live a full Jewish life by keeping the mitzvot and caring for others; some argue death and mourning rituals are equally important for honouring life.
exam.conclusion: Marriage is extremely important because it builds Jewish homes and families, but it is one of several life stages, and Jews who do not marry still live complete Jewish lives.
exam.model:
Many Jews would agree that marriage is the most important stage of life. The first command in the Torah is 'Be fruitful and multiply' (Genesis 1:28), and after creating Adam God said, 'It is not good for the man to be alone' (Genesis 2:18). The rabbis call marriage kiddushin, meaning holiness, because the couple are set apart for each other in a relationship that includes God. The Talmud even says that a man without a wife lives without joy, without blessing and without goodness (Yevamot 62b). Most importantly, much of Jewish life happens in the home: Shabbat meals, Pesach Seders and keeping kosher. Marriage creates the home where children learn their faith, so it is vital for the survival of Judaism. This is a strong argument because without Jewish families the tradition could not continue.

However, other stages could be seen as just as important. Brit Milah is commanded directly by God as the sign of the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:10-12), so it marks a Jewish boy's entry into the covenant. Bar and Bat Mitzvah is when a young person personally takes on the mitzvot, which Pirkei Avot 5:21 links to age thirteen, and this applies to every Jew whether or not they marry. Not everyone marries, and a single Jew can still live a full and holy life by keeping Shabbat, giving tzedakah and studying Torah. Mourning rituals are also important because they honour the dead and comfort the living. This is a convincing argument because Jewish law is for everyone, not just married people.

In conclusion, I partly agree. Marriage is one of the most important stages because it builds the Jewish home, where faith is lived and passed on. However, I would not call it the most important, because Brit Milah and Bar or Bat Mitzvah mark a person's relationship with the covenant itself, and Jews who do not marry are still fully part of the Jewish people.

exam.q: Explain two Jewish mourning rituals. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One ritual is quick burial. The body is washed by the Chevra Kadisha, wrapped in a plain shroud and buried in a simple coffin, usually within 24 hours. Deuteronomy 21:23 says a body should be buried the same day. This shows respect for the body that God created, and for many Orthodox Jews it is linked to belief in the resurrection, which is why they do not cremate.

Another ritual is sitting shiva for seven days after the funeral. Mourners stay at home, sit on low stools and cover mirrors, while the community visits, brings food and forms a minyan so the mourners can say Kaddish. On hearing of the death they will have said 'Blessed is the true Judge', echoing Job 1:21, 'The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away'. This means mourners are supported to grieve while still praising God.
points: Quick burial, Chevra Kadisha, plain shroud and coffin (Deuteronomy 21:23; Genesis 3:19)
Keriah: tearing clothes as a sign of grief
Shiva: seven days at home, low stools, covered mirrors, visitors
Kaddish said with a minyan for 11 months for a parent; yahrzeit
Barukh Dayan HaEmet on hearing of death (Job 1:21)
Marks: 2 per developed ritual, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: 'Jewish mourning rituals are more for the living than for the dead.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Shiva, sheloshim and the year of mourning are designed to let mourners grieve in stages and return slowly to normal life.
The community surrounds mourners with support: visits, meals, a minyan at home, and the words 'May God comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem'.
Kaddish praises God rather than mentioning the dead, helping the mourner keep faith during grief.
against: Quick burial, washing by the Chevra Kadisha and a watcher staying with the body show respect for the dead person, made in God's image.
Burying rather than cremating, for Orthodox Jews, prepares for the resurrection (Daniel 12:2), so it is for the dead.
Many believe saying Kaddish helps the soul of the dead person, which is why it is said for 11 months; shovelling earth is called the truest kindness because the dead cannot repay it.
exam.conclusion: The rituals serve both: they honour the dead and support the living, and Judaism sees these as linked acts of chesed (kindness).
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that mourning rituals are mainly for the living. The stages of mourning are carefully designed to help people grieve: seven days of shiva at home, then the thirty days of sheloshim, then a year for a parent, allowing mourners to return gradually to normal life. During shiva the community visits, brings food and forms a minyan at the mourner's home, so the bereaved are never alone. Visitors say, 'May God comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem'. The Kaddish, which mourners say daily, does not mention death at all but praises God, helping the mourner keep faith in a time of loss. This is a strong argument because these practices clearly focus on the wellbeing of those left behind.

However, other Jews would say the rituals are just as much for the dead. The body is washed with care by the Chevra Kadisha, dressed in a simple shroud and never left alone before the funeral, because it was created in the image of God. Burial happens quickly, following Deuteronomy 21:23, and many Orthodox Jews refuse cremation because they believe in the resurrection of the dead (Daniel 12:2). Many Jews believe that saying Kaddish helps the soul of the person who has died, which is why it is said for eleven months. Shovelling earth onto the coffin is seen as the purest act of kindness, because the dead person can never repay it. This is a convincing argument because it shows the rituals express respect and duty towards the dead.

In conclusion, I disagree that the rituals are more for the living. Jewish mourning practices are an act of chesed in two directions: they honour the dead person, and they comfort and support the mourners. Most Jews would see these purposes as joined together rather than one being more important than the other.

exam.q: Explain two reasons why many Jews keep the dietary laws. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One reason is that the dietary laws are commanded by God in the Torah. Leviticus 11 sets out which animals may be eaten, such as those that chew the cud and have split hooves, and Exodus 23:19 says 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk'. Many Jews, especially Orthodox Jews, keep these laws simply because God commanded them, even without a stated reason, so they keep separate dishes for meat and dairy.

Another reason is that keeping kosher makes everyday life holy. Leviticus 11:44 says 'Be holy, for I am holy'. This means every meal becomes a reminder of God and of the covenant, and it gives Jews a shared identity, because keeping kosher sets them apart and connects them to Jews all over the world.
points: Commanded by God (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14; Exodus 23:19)
Holiness: 'Be holy, for I am holy' (Leviticus 11:44)
Self-discipline and control of appetite (Maimonides)
Identity and unity; reminder of God at every meal
Respect for life: no blood (Leviticus 17:11), shechitah
Marks: 2 per developed reason, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: Explain two reasons why Yom Kippur is important for Jews. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One reason is that Yom Kippur is the Day of Atonement, when Jews believe God forgives the sins of those who sincerely repent. Leviticus 16:30 says 'on this day atonement shall be made for you to purify you of all your sins'. This is why Jews fast for 25 hours, wear white as a symbol of purity and spend the day confessing their sins in the synagogue.

Another reason is that Jews believe God's judgement for the year, written on Rosh Hashanah, is sealed at the end of Yom Kippur. The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 16b) describes books being opened for the righteous, the wicked and those in between. This means Jews use the final service, Neilah, as a last chance to return to God before the Ark is closed and the shofar is sounded.
points: Day of Atonement: forgiveness for sincere repentance (Leviticus 16:30; Leviticus 23:27)
Judgement sealed; Neilah as the last chance (Rosh Hashanah 16b)
Holiest day: fasting, white clothes, day in synagogue, Vidui
Reconciliation with others first (Mishnah Yoma 8:9)
Jonah reading shows God forgives all who repent
Marks: 2 per developed reason, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: Explain two different ways in which Jews prepare for and celebrate Pesach. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is by removing chametz from the home before the festival. Families clean the house thoroughly and search for the last crumbs by candlelight the night before, then burn or sell what is left, because the Israelites left Egypt so quickly that their bread could not rise.

A different way is by holding the Seder meal. The family reads the Haggadah, the youngest child asks the Four Questions, and they eat symbolic foods such as maror (bitter herbs) for the bitterness of slavery and matzah for the haste of leaving Egypt, so the story is passed to the next generation.
points: Preparation: cleaning, bedikat chametz, burning or selling chametz, Pesach dishes
Seder: Haggadah, Four Questions, Seder plate symbols, four cups of wine
Afikoman hunt; Elijah's cup; 'Next year in Jerusalem'
Eating matzah for the whole festival (7 or 8 days)
Orthodox: two Seders and 8 days outside Israel; Reform: often one Seder, 7 days
Each way: 1 mark simple, 2 marks detailed; ways must be different

exam.q: Explain two ways in which the Seder meal helps Jews remember the Exodus. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One way is through retelling the story. The family reads the Haggadah, and the youngest child asks the Four Questions beginning 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'. Exodus 13:8 commands parents to explain to their children what God did when the Israelites went free from Egypt. This means the story is passed on to every new generation, so children grow up knowing God saved their ancestors.

Another way is through the symbolic foods. Rabban Gamaliel taught in the Mishnah (Pesachim 10:5) that anyone who has not explained the Passover offering, the matzah and the maror has not done their duty. Matzah recalls the haste of leaving Egypt, maror the bitterness of slavery and charoset the mortar the slaves used. Tasting these foods helps Jews feel 'as if they personally came out of Egypt'.
points: Retelling with the Haggadah and the Four Questions (Exodus 13:8; Exodus 12:26-27)
Symbolic foods: matzah, maror, charoset, karpas in salt water, zeroa, beitzah (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5)
Four cups of wine linked to God's promises of freedom (Exodus 6:6-7)
Removing drops of wine for the plagues; Elijah's cup; 'Next year in Jerusalem'
Seeing oneself as personally freed from Egypt
Marks: 2 per developed way, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: 'Pesach is the most important festival for Jews in Britain today.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Pesach remembers the Exodus, when God freed the Israelites and made them a people; it is commanded 'for all time' (Exodus 12:14).
It is one of the most widely kept festivals in Britain: many Jews who keep little else attend a family Seder, so it unites the community.
It passes faith to children (Exodus 13:8) and its message of freedom is relevant today, with readings about refugees and modern slavery.
against: Yom Kippur is called the holiest day of the year; many British Jews who rarely attend synagogue go on Yom Kippur to seek forgiveness (Leviticus 16:30).
Rosh Hashanah begins the year with judgement and the Ten Days of Awe, shaping a Jew's relationship with God for the whole year.
Shabbat happens every week and is one of the Ten Commandments, so for observant Jews it shapes life more than any yearly festival.
exam.conclusion: Pesach may be the most widely celebrated festival in Britain because of its family focus and message of freedom, but in terms of holiness Yom Kippur is usually seen as the most important, so it depends whether importance means popularity or holiness.
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that Pesach is the most important festival. It remembers the Exodus, when God freed the Israelites from slavery and turned them into a people, which is the foundation of Jewish identity. The Torah commands Jews to keep it 'for all time' (Exodus 12:14), and Exodus 13:8 tells parents to explain the story to their children. In Britain, Pesach is one of the most widely kept festivals: many Jews who rarely go to synagogue still attend a family Seder, read the Haggadah and eat matzah. Its message of freedom also speaks to modern Britain, and many families add readings about refugees or modern slavery. This is a strong argument because Pesach reaches the most people and passes the faith to the next generation.

However, others would argue that Yom Kippur is more important. It is the Day of Atonement, when Leviticus 16:30 says atonement is made to purify the people of their sins, and Jews believe God's judgement for the year is sealed. It is called the holiest day of the year, and British synagogues are at their fullest, with many Jews fasting for 25 hours. Rosh Hashanah could also be seen as more important because it starts the Ten Days of Awe and celebrates the creation of the world. Others would point out that Shabbat, one of the Ten Commandments, happens every week, so for observant Jews it shapes life far more than a yearly festival. This is a convincing argument because it focuses on the relationship with God rather than on family tradition.

In conclusion, I think it depends on what 'important' means. If it means the festival most widely celebrated by British Jews, Pesach has a strong claim because of its family focus. But in terms of holiness and the relationship with God, Yom Kippur is usually seen as the most important day, so I would not fully agree with the statement.
